    Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam 11.7.1

    The Supreme Personality of Godhead said: O greatly fortunate Uddhava, you have accurately revealed My desire to withdraw the Yadu dynasty from the earth and return to My own abode in Vaikuṇṭha. Thus Lord Brahmā, Lord Śiva and all other planetary rulers are now praying for Me to resume My residence in Vaikuṇṭha.
    Purport

    Each and every demigod has his particular abode in the heavenly planets within the material universe. Although Lord Viṣṇu is sometimes counted among the demigods, His abode is in Vaikuṇṭha, the spiritual sky. The demigods are universal controllers within the kingdom of māyā, but Viṣṇu is the Lord of the illusory potency and many other spiritual potencies. His exalted residence does not lie within the kingdom of His insignificant maidservant māyā.

    Lord Viṣṇu, the Personality of Godhead, is the Supreme Lord of all lords; the demigods are His separated parts and parcels. Being themselves minute jīva souls, the demigods are under the influence of the potency of māyā; but Lord Viṣṇu is always the supreme controller of māyā. The Personality of Godhead is the reservoir and root of all existence, and the material world is just a dim reflection of the brilliant scenery of His eternal, spiritual abode, where everything is infinitely beautiful and pleasurable. Viṣṇu is the supreme reality, and no living entity can ever be equal to or greater than Him. The Lord exists within His own unique category called viṣṇu-tattva, or the Supreme Personality of Godhead. All other prominent or extraordinary living entities owe their positions and potencies to the Lord. Ultimately Viṣṇu Himself is a plenary expansion of Lord Kṛṣṇa, the original source of all the viṣṇu-tattva and jīva-tattva expansions. Thus Lord Kṛṣṇa is the basis of everything.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    The Supreme Lord said: O greatly fortunate Uddhava! You have accurately revealed my desire to withdraw the Yadu dynasty from the earth and return to my own abode in Vaikuṇṭha. Thus Brahmā, Śiva and all other planetary rulers are now praying for me to resume my residence in Vaikuṇṭha. In the Seventh Chapter, desiring to give Uddhava jṣāna and vairāgya, Kṛṣṇa speaks of the various gurus starting with the earth, mentioned by the avadhūta. Svar-vāsam means “to Vaikuṇṭha.”

    Personal Guidance
    Kṛṣṇa confirms His own desire to withdraw the Yadus and return to Vaikuṇṭha — even the universal rulers must defer to the Lord's sovereign plan.
    Practical Applications
    • Name one situation today where you are quietly resisting an ending Kṛṣṇa is clearly closing, and stop arguing with the timing.
    • When you pray, drop the demand-tone and align your asking with what the Lord is already doing in your life this week.
    • Refuse the temptation to treat any controller — boss, government, even a respected demigod-like figure — as the ultimate authority over your situation.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where am I praying for Kṛṣṇa to stay within an arrangement He is signalling He wants to dissolve, and what attachment is driving that request?
    • If even Brahmā and Śiva position themselves as petitioners before Viṣṇu, where am I still quietly placing myself above that posture in my own life?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • When a friendship or group is clearly ending — a graduating class, a club, a shared house — stop praying for it to last and start asking how to leave it cleanly.
    • Notice when you treat a professor, coach, or online figure as a final authority on your life, and remember even Brahmā and Śiva are petitioners before the Lord.
    • Before exam season, frame your study not as a demand on Kṛṣṇa for a result but as cooperation with what He is already arranging for your next stage.
    householder
    • When a job, a house, or a phase of family life is visibly closing, audit which prayers of yours are really arguments with the Lord's timing, and drop them.
    • In family decisions, refuse to make any human controller — in-laws, employer, government — the ultimate reference point; check the choice against Kṛṣṇa's stated will first.
    • Model for your children that even great powers in this world are praying upward, so they grow up locating final authority in the Lord, not in worldly success.
    senior
    • When peers pray loudly for your health or longevity, internally align instead with whatever withdrawal or remaining the Lord is indicating for you.
    • Loosen your grip on legacies — institutions, properties, even disciples — remembering that the Lord arranges arrivals and departures on His own schedule.
    • Mentor younger devotees into the posture of Brahmā and Śiva in this verse: petitioning, not commanding; cooperating with Kṛṣṇa's withdrawals, not resisting them.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Reading the verse as cosmic trivia about demigods instead of as a personal instruction to align with the Lord's withdrawing and revealing movements in your own life.
    • Flattening Viṣṇu into one more powerful being on the same scale as Brahmā and Śiva, instead of recognizing the viṣṇu-tattva category as wholly distinct.
    • Using the Lord's sovereign plan as an excuse for passivity — "it is all His will" — rather than for active, surrendered cooperation with what He is doing.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Share a time you prayed hard for something to continue, and later realized Kṛṣṇa was kindly ending it — what changed in your prayer after that?
    • Why does Prabhupāda insist on the distinction between Viṣṇu and the demigods here, and where in modern spiritual culture do you see that distinction collapsed?
    • If even Brahmā and Śiva are praying for the Lord to resume His abode, what does that tell you about the limits of any institution, lineage, or leader you currently rely on?
    Role Play

    One student plays a senior devotee who is being asked by community members to pray that a beloved guru's life be extended; another plays a younger devotee who senses the guru himself wishes to depart. Work through the conversation in light of this verse — how to honor affection without praying against the Lord's clearly indicated desire.

    Objections & Responses
    • If Kṛṣṇa was always going to withdraw the Yadus anyway, Uddhava's perception and the demigods' prayers are just theater — why bother praying at all?
      The Lord's plan is sovereign, but He delights in the conscious participation of His devotees. Uddhava's accurate reading and the demigods' prayers are not what cause the withdrawal — they are the loving recognition that lets them move with Him rather than be left behind by Him. Surrendered prayer aligns the heart with what Kṛṣṇa is doing; it is never a lever to override Him.
    • Treating Viṣṇu as categorically above Brahmā and Śiva sounds sectarian — aren't all these just names for one Absolute?
      Prabhupāda's purport is precise here: Brahmā and Śiva are jīvas under māyā's influence, while Viṣṇu is the Lord of māyā and stands in His own category, viṣṇu-tattva. This is not sectarian preference; it is the structural difference between a servant of the potency and the master of the potency. Collapsing that distinction is exactly the impersonalist drift the Gauḍīya line is meant to correct.

    Answering the prayer of Lord Brahmā, I descended within this world along with My plenary portion, Lord Baladeva, and performed various activities on behalf of the demigods. I have now completed My mission here.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Answering the prayer of Brahmā, I descended within this world along with my portion, Baladeva, and performed various activities on behalf of the devatās. I have now completed my mission here. Aṁśena means “with Balarāma.”
    Related lectures
    • Tamohara Pr SB 11-07-02-03 - 2017-03-09 ISKCON Alachua
      His Grace Tamohara Prabhu· 2017-03-09· English
    Personal Guidance
    Kṛṣṇa descends in answer to prayer, accomplishes the deva-kārya completely, then withdraws — His mission, not ours, sets the timing.
    Practical Applications
    • Name one task today that you treat as 'your' mission, and consciously re-frame it as service offered upward to Kṛṣṇa, who alone completes anything.
    • When a prayer of yours seems unanswered, refuse the conclusion that He is absent — He descends in answer to sincere prayer in His own time and form.
    • At day's end, audit what you 'finished' and acknowledge that completion (aśeṣataḥ) belongs to Him; offer the day's results and release them.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where am I quietly resenting that Kṛṣṇa's mission in my life is not on my timetable, and what does His aśeṣataḥ — complete on His side — ask me to surrender?
    • If even Kṛṣṇa descends only when prayed for, what prayer have I been postponing, and what does that postponement reveal about my real refuge?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • Before an exam or audition you've been praying about, remember Brahmā had to ask — practice actually asking Kṛṣṇa, in your own words, instead of only worrying.
    • When a friend group or social media moment feels like 'your big mission,' check whether you're inflating ordinary work with Kṛṣṇa-sized language; keep the scale honest.
    • If a prayer of yours seems ignored, refuse the cynic's conclusion that no one is listening — His timing for descent is His, not yours, even at your age.
    householder
    • Name the family project (a move, a child's schooling, a career pivot) you secretly treat as 'my mission'; rename it as service and pray, like Brahmā, for Kṛṣṇa to enter it.
    • When you finish a long-running responsibility, refuse the proud 'I did it' — offer the aśeṣataḥ to Him and notice how much lighter the next responsibility becomes.
    • Speak with your spouse this week about one decision you've been making by spreadsheet alone, and bring it into prayer before any further step.
    senior
    • Look back on the 'missions' of your life — career, raising children, building a home — and name which you still cling to as yours rather than His already-completed work.
    • When the body signals that your time here is winding down, take this verse as your own template: mission on His terms, departure on His terms, no anxiety.
    • Mentor one younger person specifically on the practice of praying for Kṛṣṇa's descent into a situation, rather than strategizing alone.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Reading the verse as His exit from history, and quietly concluding He is no longer accessible — forgetting that the holy name and the sādhu-saṅga are His continued descent.
    • Imagining one's own work as a parallel 'mission accomplished,' inflating ahaṅkāra by borrowing Kṛṣṇa's language for ordinary karma.
    • Hearing 'on behalf of the demigods' and drifting toward demigod-confusion — as if Kṛṣṇa is one functionary among many, rather than the source whom even Brahmā petitions.
    Discussion Prompts
    • If Kṛṣṇa says His work here is finished, in what sense is He still acting in our lives today — and where do we disagree about what counts as His action?
    • Brahmā had to pray for the descent. What does this say about whether our prayers actually move anything, and where does that idea make us uncomfortable?
    • What is the difference between Kṛṣṇa's 'mission complete' (aśeṣataḥ) and our restless sense that our own work is never done?
    Role Play

    A senior devotee tells a younger one, 'Kṛṣṇa already finished His work on earth — we're just living in the aftermath, so don't expect any personal intervention.' One student plays the senior, another plays a sincere new student who feels this drains hope from sādhana; a teacher coaches the new student to respond from this verse without dismissing the senior's point about aśeṣataḥ.

    Objections & Responses
    • If Kṛṣṇa has already 'completed His mission' and withdrawn, this verse sounds like a polite goodbye — why should a modern person bother praying to someone who has closed the office?
      The verse describes the completion of one specific deva-kārya, not the end of His accessibility. Brahmā's prayer brought the descent; our prayer — through the holy name, the Bhāgavatam, and sādhu-saṅga — continues to draw Him near. He withdrew the form, not the relationship.
    • Saying Kṛṣṇa descended 'on behalf of the demigods' makes Him sound like staff sent to handle a request — hardly the Supreme.
      Notice who is petitioning whom. Brahmā, the first created being, prays; Kṛṣṇa, the original Person, chooses to descend with His own plenary portion. The demigods are dependents seeking shelter, not employers — His response is mercy, not obligation, and that is precisely what marks Him as Supreme.

    • What is the difference between Kṛṣṇa's 'mission complete' (aśeṣataḥ) and our restless sense that our own work is never done?
    Role Play

    A senior devotee tells a younger one, 'Kṛṣṇa already finished His work on earth — we're just living in the aftermath, so don't expect any personal intervention.' One student plays the senior, another plays a sincere new student who feels this drains hope from sādhana; a teacher coaches the new student to respond from this verse without dismissing the senior's point about aśeṣataḥ.

    Objections & Responses
    • If Kṛṣṇa has already 'completed His mission' and withdrawn, this verse sounds like a polite goodbye — why should a modern person bother praying to someone who has closed the office?
      The verse describes the completion of one specific deva-kārya, not the end of His accessibility. Brahmā's prayer brought the descent; our prayer — through the holy name, the Bhāgavatam, and sādhu-saṅga — continues to draw Him near. He withdrew the form, not the relationship.
    • Saying Kṛṣṇa descended 'on behalf of the demigods' makes Him sound like staff sent to handle a request — hardly the Supreme.
      Notice who is petitioning whom. Brahmā, the first created being, prays; Kṛṣṇa, the original Person, chooses to descend with His own plenary portion. The demigods are dependents seeking shelter, not employers — His response is mercy, not obligation, and that is precisely what marks Him as Supreme.
    📝 My note

    Source: vedabase.io

    Now due to the brāhmaṇas’ curse the Yadu dynasty will certainly perish by fighting among themselves; and on the seventh day from today the ocean will rise up and inundate this city of Dvārakā.
    Purport

    In this and the following verses, Lord Kṛṣṇa indicates to Uddhava that he should immediately fix himself in self-realization by giving up all identification with the material world. Śrīla Jīva Gosvāmī has pointed out that the Yadu dynasty was not actually destroyed by Lord Kṛṣṇa but merely removed from the vision of the world through the curse of the brāhmaṇas; similarly, the Lord’s eternal abode Dvārakā can never be drowned by the ocean. Nevertheless, all external approaches to this transcendental city were covered by the ocean, and thus the Lord’s abode remains inaccessible to foolish persons in Kali-yuga, as will be described later in this canto.

    By the Lord’s mystic potency, called yoga-māyā, He reveals His own form, abode, paraphernalia, pastimes, entourage, and so on, and at the suitable time He removes all of these from our mundane sight. Although bewildered conditioned souls may doubt the spiritual potency of the Lord, the pure devotees can directly perceive and relish His transcendental appearance and disappearance, which are described in Bhagavad-gītā as janma karma ca me divyam. If one faithfully accepts this perfect knowledge of the Lord’s transcendental nature, then surely one will go back home, back to Godhead, and become an eternal companion of Lord Kṛṣṇa.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Now, due to the brāhmaṇas’ curse, the Yadu dynasty will certainly perish by fighting among themselves; and on the seventh day from today the ocean will rise up and inundate this city of Dvārakā.
    Related lectures
    • RGS SB 11-07-03-11 Hindi - Twenty-Four Guru-08
      His Holiness Radha Govinda Swami· English
    Personal Guidance
    Kṛṣṇa signals Uddhava that the visible world — even Dvārakā and the Yadus — will be withdrawn; fix yourself in Him before the props fall.
    Practical Applications
    • Name one external arrangement — job, home, relationship — you secretly treat as permanent, and today act as though Kṛṣṇa could withdraw it within a week.
    • Before sleep, mentally release the people and places of your day back to Kṛṣṇa, refusing to grip them as yours.
    • Spend ten minutes reading or hearing about Kṛṣṇa's transcendental form and abode, so the inner anchor deepens while outer scenery shifts.
    Reflection Questions
    • If I were told the city, family, or institution I lean on would be 'covered over' in seven days, what unfinished surrender would I scramble to make?
    • Where am I mistaking the visible disappearance of something for its real destruction, the way foolish onlookers misread Dvārakā's submergence?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • Pick the friend group, college plan, or follower count you assume will still be there next year, and act today as if Kṛṣṇa could quietly remove it.
    • When a result you wanted — a grade, a relationship, a selection — disappears, refuse the story that your life is over; treat it as one Dvārakā being covered, not destroyed.
    • Cut ten minutes from scrolling and spend it hearing about Kṛṣṇa's form and pastimes, so something real is being built while everything outside keeps shifting.
    householder
    • Name the career position, house, or family configuration you most quietly cling to, and consciously offer it back to Kṛṣṇa before making this week's decisions about it.
    • Talk with your spouse about what would actually need to be in place — sādhana, finances, children's training — if the outer arrangements you depend on were withdrawn within a year.
    • Lead one family activity this week — kīrtana, reading, offering food — that strengthens what cannot be taken by 'ocean or fighting,' rather than only what the world can confiscate.
    senior
    • Identify one possession, role, or recognition you are still holding as 'mine,' and begin a deliberate handover, treating it as already withdrawn from your vision.
    • Speak with a younger person this week about Kṛṣṇa's eternal abode, so that what you leave behind is not only assets but the knowledge that nothing real is lost.
    • When the body, memory, or social standing visibly diminishes, anchor in the truth that disappearance from mundane sight is not annihilation, and use the time to deepen remembrance of Kṛṣṇa.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Reading the verse as a cosmic disaster story rather than as Kṛṣṇa's personal instruction to fix oneself in self-realization now.
    • Concluding that the Yadus and Dvārakā were truly destroyed, missing Jīva Gosvāmī's point that they were only removed from mundane vision.
    • Using the certainty of impermanence as an excuse for fatalism or neglect of duty, instead of for sharper, detached engagement.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Share one arrangement in your life you have been treating as Dvārakā-permanent — and what would change tomorrow if you accepted it could be withdrawn.
    • Jīva Gosvāmī says the dynasty and city were not destroyed but hidden from view; where in your own life have you confused 'no longer visible to me' with 'gone forever'?
    • Kṛṣṇa uses an impending catastrophe to push Uddhava into self-realization — is fear of loss a legitimate doorway to bhakti, or a shaky foundation? Disagree honestly.
    Role Play

    One student plays Uddhava, just told that within seven days the Yadus will fight to the death and the ocean will swallow Dvārakā. Another plays a worldly friend urging him to organize defenses, evacuate families, and save the city. Uddhava must respond from the verse's actual instruction — fix yourself in self-realization — without sounding callous, and the friend must press hard on why that looks like abandonment.

    Objections & Responses
    • This sounds fatalistic — Kṛṣṇa announces destruction and tells Uddhava to withdraw inward rather than help. Isn't that spiritual escapism?
      Uddhava is not told to abandon responsibility but to stop identifying with what is about to be withdrawn from view. Kṛṣṇa is preparing His confidential servant for continued service in full knowledge, not for passivity; real compassion serves the soul, and Uddhava's later mission depends on this inner fixing.
    • If Dvārakā was not really destroyed, why does the verse plainly say the ocean will inundate it? This feels like reinterpreting scripture to protect a doctrine.
      The verse and the ācāryas are not in conflict — externally the ocean did rise and cover the approaches, exactly as said; internally the eternal abode is untouched, as Jīva Gosvāmī clarifies. Both layers are needed: the historical event teaches detachment, the transcendental fact teaches that Kṛṣṇa's līlā and dhāma are never lost.

    O saintly Uddhava, in the near future I will abandon this earth. Then, being overwhelmed by the Age of Kali, the earth will be bereft of all piety.
    Purport

    Lord Kṛṣṇa’s plan was to bring Uddhava back to His own eternal abode after a brief delay. Because of Uddhava’s extraordinary spiritual qualities, the Lord wanted to engage him in propagating His message among other saintly persons who were not yet advanced to the stage of pure devotional service. However, the Lord assured Uddhava that he would not be bereft of the Lord’s association for even a moment. Also, because Uddhava had become a perfect master of his senses, he would never be afflicted by the three modes of material nature. In this way, before bringing Uddhava back home, back to Godhead, the Lord empowered him to carry out a specific confidential mission.

    Wherever the supreme position of the Personality of Godhead is not recognized, useless mental speculation becomes very prominent, and the safe and sure path of hearing perfect Vedic knowledge becomes covered by the chaos of mental concoction. At the present time, especially in the Western countries, literally millions of books are being published on hundreds and thousands of subjects; yet despite this proliferation of mental concoction people remain totally in ignorance about the most fundamental issues of human life, namely, Who am I? Where have I come from? Where am I going? What is my soul? What is God?

    The Personality of Godhead, Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa, is the reservoir of innumerable enchanting pastimes, and thus He is the source of innumerable varieties of pleasure. In fact, He is the ocean of eternal pleasure. When the eternal soul is bereft of the constitutional pleasure that comes from loving service to the Lord, he is overwhelmed and bewildered by material nature. He helplessly chases after material sense gratification, thinking that one material object is good and another bad, and constantly changes his assessment of what is good and what is bad. Thus he derives no peace or pleasure, is in constant anxiety and is repeatedly thrashed by the cruel laws of nature in the form of birth, death, old age and disease.

    In this way the conditioned soul becomes a fit candidate to take birth in Kali-yuga, which is the epitome of misfortune. In Kali-yuga the living entities, who are already suffering so many tribulations, mercilessly turn against one another. Human society in Kali-yuga becomes savagely violent, and men open slaughterhouses to butcher hundreds of millions of innocent creatures. Large-scale wars are declared, and millions of human beings, even women and children, are quickly annihilated.

    Unless the living entity recognizes the authority of the Personality of Godhead, he remains a helpless victim in the clutches of māyā, or material illusion. He concocts different solutions to release himself from māyā, but these solutions are themselves creations of māyā and thus cannot possibly release the conditioned soul. In fact, they only intensify his distress. In the next verse, Lord Kṛṣṇa specifically warns Uddhava to avoid Kali-yuga and go back home, back to Godhead. Those of us who have already taken birth in Kali-yuga should also heed this advice and immediately take all necessary steps to go back to the Lord’s eternal abode for a blissful life of perfect knowledge. The material world is never a happy place, especially during the fearful days of Kali-yuga.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    O saintly Uddhava! In the near future I will abandon this earth. Then, being overwhelmed by the age of Kali, the earth will be bereft of all auspiciousness.

    • Janmastami Pr SB 11-07-04 - 2017-03-10 ISKCON Alachua
      His Grace Janmastami Prabhu· 2017-03-10· English
    • MG SB 11-07-04 - Love minus lust is pure love - 2006-12-16 Rajkot
      His Holiness Mahavishnu Goswami· 2006-12-16· English
    Personal Guidance
    Kṛṣṇa is about to leave the earth, and Kali-yuga will strip it of piety — so urgently take shelter of Him now while we still can.
    Practical Applications
    • Name one Kali-yuga current — distraction, cynicism, sense gratification — pulling at you today and consciously refuse it once.
    • Spend ten uninterrupted minutes hearing or chanting Kṛṣṇa's names this morning, treating it as the lifeline Kṛṣṇa Himself extends.
    • Identify one place where you have been waiting for 'better conditions' to become serious about bhakti, and begin today instead.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where am I assuming the world will give me time and stability to take bhakti seriously later, when the verse says the opposite?
    • What 'piety' that once steadied my life has quietly eroded under the pressure of Kali, and what would it take to recover it?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • Notice how much of your attention each day is being shaped by feeds, trends, and peer opinion — Kali's three favorite tools — and reclaim one hour for hearing about Kṛṣṇa instead.
    • Refuse the assumption that you have decades to 'get spiritual later' after career and relationships settle; begin a simple daily sādhana today, even if just chanting on the walk to class.
    • When friends mock seriousness about Kṛṣṇa as old-fashioned, do not argue — quietly continue, knowing the verse names this exact pressure as the signature of the age.
    householder
    • Build at least one Kṛṣṇa-conscious habit into the family rhythm — a verse before dinner, a Sunday hearing — so the home itself becomes a small island of piety against the surrounding age.
    • When career or financial anxiety convinces you that bhakti must wait until things stabilize, recognize that voice as Kali's, and offer the day's work to Kṛṣṇa even in the middle of the uncertainty.
    • Guard what your children consume — entertainment, food, company — not as paranoid restriction but as the practical work of raising souls in an age that will not protect them for you.
    senior
    • Use the loosening grip of career and bodily strength as Kṛṣṇa's gift: redirect those freed hours into hearing, chanting, and serving His devotees, treating this stage as designed for going back to Him.
    • Speak openly with younger family members about Kṛṣṇa and the impermanence the verse names — not as lecture but as the legacy only an elder can leave.
    • Stop waiting for the 'right' inner state to surrender; with less life remaining, take the verse's urgency personally and take shelter of Kṛṣṇa today, not at some imagined later peak.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Reading this as a cultural pessimism about modern times rather than as a personal summons to take shelter of Kṛṣṇa now.
    • Becoming fearful or paralyzed by Kali-yuga's symptoms instead of acting on Kṛṣṇa's prescription to go back to Him.
    • Imagining one can stay neutral — neither sinking with Kali nor surrendering to Kṛṣṇa — when the verse forecloses that middle ground.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Share one specific symptom of Kali-yuga you see in your own daily life, not the world at large — and where you have been complicit in it.
    • Kṛṣṇa says the earth will be bereft of piety once He withdraws — what, then, do you understand as the actual source of piety in your life?
    • Do you experience these as 'fearful days of Kali-yuga,' or do they feel ordinary? Discuss honestly what that says about your spiritual urgency.
    Role Play

    One student plays a busy professional who insists Kali-yuga talk is medieval doom-mongering and that the modern world is better than ever — longer lives, less violence, more comfort. Another student, as a sincere Gauḍīya practitioner, has fifteen minutes to respond not by arguing statistics but by drawing the conversation back to the verse's central point: that without recognition of the Personality of Godhead, the soul is helplessly tossed by material nature regardless of outward comfort.

    Objections & Responses
    • This sounds like apocalyptic thinking. Every age complains about its own decline — why should I treat Kali-yuga as anything but cultural pessimism?
      The verse is not nostalgia for a lost golden age; it is Kṛṣṇa's own diagnosis of what happens when His supreme position is forgotten. The test is not whether technology improves but whether the soul finds peace — and Prabhupāda points to the constant anxiety, the slaughterhouses, the mass wars as evidence we are not getting freer, only more efficient at suffering.
    • If Kṛṣṇa knew Kali-yuga would be this bad, why did He leave at all? It seems unfair to abandon us to it.
      He did not abandon us — He left His name, His instructions, and His devotees, and in this age He descends as the holy name itself. The verse is meant to wake us up to use what He has left, not to mourn what He withdrew; the very fact that we are hearing this verse is evidence of His ongoing mercy.

    • Becoming fearful or paralyzed by Kali-yuga's symptoms instead of acting on Kṛṣṇa's prescription to go back to Him.
    • Imagining one can stay neutral — neither sinking with Kali nor surrendering to Kṛṣṇa — when the verse forecloses that middle ground.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Share one specific symptom of Kali-yuga you see in your own daily life, not the world at large — and where you have been complicit in it.
    • Kṛṣṇa says the earth will be bereft of piety once He withdraws — what, then, do you understand as the actual source of piety in your life?
    • Do you experience these as 'fearful days of Kali-yuga,' or do they feel ordinary? Discuss honestly what that says about your spiritual urgency.
    Role Play

    One student plays a busy professional who insists Kali-yuga talk is medieval doom-mongering and that the modern world is better than ever — longer lives, less violence, more comfort. Another student, as a sincere Gauḍīya practitioner, has fifteen minutes to respond not by arguing statistics but by drawing the conversation back to the verse's central point: that without recognition of the Personality of Godhead, the soul is helplessly tossed by material nature regardless of outward comfort.

    Objections & Responses
    • This sounds like apocalyptic thinking. Every age complains about its own decline — why should I treat Kali-yuga as anything but cultural pessimism?
      The verse is not nostalgia for a lost golden age; it is Kṛṣṇa's own diagnosis of what happens when His supreme position is forgotten. The test is not whether technology improves but whether the soul finds peace — and Prabhupāda points to the constant anxiety, the slaughterhouses, the mass wars as evidence we are not getting freer, only more efficient at suffering.
    • If Kṛṣṇa knew Kali-yuga would be this bad, why did He leave at all? It seems unfair to abandon us to it.
      He did not abandon us — He left His name, His instructions, and His devotees, and in this age He descends as the holy name itself. The verse is meant to wake us up to use what He has left, not to mourn what He withdrew; the very fact that we are hearing this verse is evidence of His ongoing mercy.

    My dear Uddhava, you should not remain here on the earth once I have abandoned this world. My dear devotee, you are sinless, but in Kali-yuga the people will be addicted to all types of sinful activities; therefore do not stay here.
    Purport

    In this Age of Kali, human beings are totally unaware that the Supreme Personality of Godhead comes personally to the earth to manifest His transcendental pastimes as they are enacted in the spiritual world. Heedless of the authority of the Personality of Godhead, the fallen souls of Kali-yuga become engulfed in bitter quarrel and cruelly harass one another. Because people in Kali-yuga are addicted to polluted, sinful activities, they are always angry, lusty and frustrated. In Kali-yuga the devotees of the Personality of Godhead, who are engaged in the ever-increasing loving service of the Lord, should never be attracted to living on the earth, the population of which is covered in the darkness of ignorance and devoid of any loving relationship with the Lord. Thus Lord Kṛṣṇa advised Uddhava not to remain on the earth in Kali-yuga. In fact, in Bhagavad-gītā the Lord advises all living entities that they should never remain anywhere within the material universe — during any age. Therefore every living being should take advantage of the pressures of Kali-yuga to understand the overall useless nature of the material world and surrender himself at the lotus feet of Lord Kṛṣṇa. Following in the footsteps of Śrī Uddhava, one should surrender to Kṛṣṇa and go back home, back to Godhead.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    You should not remain here on the earth once I have abandoned this world. O sinless devotee! In Kali-yuga the people will be addicted to all types of sinful activities.
    Personal Guidance
    Kali-yuga's populace is addicted to sinful activity; do not settle into this world — take its pressures as a goad to surrender to Kṛṣṇa.
    Practical Applications
    • Notice one specific way the surrounding culture has normalized anger, lust, or frustration in you today, and refuse to participate in it.
    • Treat each pressure or disappointment of Kali-yuga as a direct nudge to deepen your sādhana rather than a problem to be optimized away.
    • Before sleep, formally offer the day at Kṛṣṇa's lotus feet and re-affirm that this world is not your final residence.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where am I quietly trying to build a permanent home in a world that Kṛṣṇa Himself told Uddhava to leave?
    • Which of Kali-yuga's pressures — quarrel, lust, anger, frustration — am I still mistaking for personal problems instead of cues to surrender?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • Audit your feeds for one week and unfollow accounts that cultivate quarrel, lust, or frustration — the very symptoms Kṛṣṇa names in this age.
    • When peers normalize cruelty, gossip, or cynicism as "just how things are," quietly refuse to join in and notice how that small refusal protects your inner life.
    • Pick one daily anchor — japa, a verse, a morning offering — that reminds you this campus, job, or city is not your permanent address.
    householder
    • Make at least one family decision this week — about money, schooling, or entertainment — explicitly weighed against whether it cultivates bhadra or abhadra taste in your children.
    • Refuse to import workplace habits of anger, competition, and frustration into the home; let the home be a small island that does not belong to Kali-yuga.
    • Treat career setbacks and social disappointments as Kṛṣṇa's reminder that you are not meant to settle here, and channel that sting into more attentive sādhana, not more striving.
    senior
    • Use the loosening grip of health, status, and ambition as confirmation of this verse — you were never meant to remain — and consciously turn each loss into renunciation rather than grief.
    • Spend deliberate time mentoring younger devotees on how to live in Kali-yuga without absorbing its tastes, passing on what experience has taught you.
    • Order your remaining years around going back to Kṛṣṇa: simplify possessions, deepen japa, and let your daily rhythm rehearse the departure Kṛṣṇa asked of Uddhava.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Reading the verse as world-hating escapism rather than a sober diagnosis that redirects energy toward bhakti.
    • Using "this is Kali-yuga" as a fatalistic excuse to lower one's own standard of sādhana and character.
    • Concluding that one must physically flee society, instead of internally refusing to belong to its abhadra-ruci (taste for the inauspicious).
    Discussion Prompts
    • Share one feature of contemporary life you had until now considered neutral but, in light of this verse, now see as abhadra-ruci — and where your group disagrees.
    • Kṛṣṇa calls Uddhava sinless yet still tells him to leave — what does this say about the danger of mere proximity to a degraded culture, and do you agree?
    • If we cannot literally leave the earth, what does "not remaining here" concretely mean for a working devotee — and where do members of the group draw that line differently?
    Role Play

    One student plays a devotee who has just been offered a high-paying role at a company whose culture thrives on quarrel, ambition, and indulgence; another plays a senior Vaiṣṇava friend. Using this verse, the friend must counsel them — neither romanticizing renunciation nor rubber-stamping the offer — on how to relate to such an environment without belonging to it.

    Objections & Responses
    • This sounds like world-denying pessimism — surely every age has had its problems, and calling our age uniquely sinful is just nostalgia for an imagined past.
      The verse is not nostalgia but Kṛṣṇa's own diagnosis spoken to Uddhava; it does not deny that good souls exist now, it warns that the ambient taste of the age is abhadra and will pull even sincere people down unless they consciously take shelter of Him.
    • If Kṛṣṇa tells His devotee to leave, are householders and working people simply stuck in a hopeless situation?
      Not at all — the same Lord who tells Uddhava to depart also gives us nāma-saṅkīrtana and the association of devotees as the way to live in Kali-yuga without being of it; the instruction is to refuse inner residence in this culture, not to abandon one's duties.

    Word-for-word

    Now you should completely give up all attachment to your personal friends and relatives and fix your mind on Me. Thus being always conscious of Me, you should observe all things with equal vision and wander throughout the earth.
    Purport

    Śrīmad Vīrarāghava Ācārya has explained the concept of equal vision as follows: sama-dṛk sarvasya brahmātmakatvānusandhāna-rūpa-sama-dṛṣṭimān. “One who is on the path of self-realization should always endeavor to see the ultimate spiritual nature of all existence.” The word mayi in this verse means paramātmani. One should fix one’s mind on the Supreme Personality of Godhead, who is the source of everything. Thus as one passes one’s life on the earth, using up one’s allotted time, one should practice seeing all things and all people as part and parcel of the Absolute Truth, the Personality of Godhead. Since all living entities are part and parcel of Kṛṣṇa, ultimately they all have the same spiritual status. The material nature, also being an emanation of Kṛṣṇa, has a similar spiritual status, but although matter and spirit are both emanations from the Personality of Godhead, they do not exist exactly on the same level. In Bhagavad-gītā it is said that the spirit soul is the superior energy of the Lord, whereas the material nature is His inferior energy. However, since Lord Kṛṣṇa is equally present in all things, the word sama-dṛk in this verse indicates that one must ultimately see Kṛṣṇa within everything and everything within Kṛṣṇa. Thus equal vision is compatible with mature knowledge of the varieties present within this world.

    Śrīla Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura comments as follows on this verse. “At the end of His manifest pastimes on the earth, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Kṛṣṇa, thought as follows within His mind: ‘During My pastimes on the earth, I have satisfied the desires of all those devotees who anxiously desired to see Me. I have duly married many thousands of queens, headed by Rukmiṇī, whom I personally kidnapped, and I have killed innumerable demons in various places and by various means. I have attended meetings, reunions and ceremonies with many friends, relatives and well-wishers in cities such as Vṛndāvana, Mathurā, Dvārakā, Hastināpura and Mithilā, and thus I have kept constantly busy coming and going in the performance of pastimes.

    “‘I further arranged to give My personal association to great devotees who are situated below the earthly planet. In order to please My mother Devakī and return her six deceased sons who were killed by Kaṁsa, I descended to the planet Sutala and blessed My great devotee Bali Mahārāja. In order to return the dead son of My spiritual master, Sāndīpani Muni, I personally went to the court of Ravinandana, or Yamarāja, and thus he was able to see Me face to face. I even blessed the residents of heaven, such as mother Aditi and Kaśyapa Muni, with My personal association when I traveled there to steal the pārijāta flower for My wife Satyabhāmā. And in order to please the inhabitants of Mahā-Viṣṇu’s abode, such as Nanda, Sunanda and Sudarśana, I traveled to Mahā-Vaikuṇṭhaloka to recover the deceased children of a frustrated brāhmaṇa. Thus, innumerable devotees who ardently desired to see Me have received the object of their prayers.

    “‘Unfortunately Nara-Nārāyaṇa Ṛṣi and the great paramahaṁsa sages who live with Him in Badarikāśrama, although most enthusiastic to see Me, never had their desire fulfilled. I have been on the earth for 125 years, and the scheduled time is now up. Being busily engaged in My pastimes, I did not have time to give My blessings to these great sages. Nevertheless, Uddhava is practically the same as Me. He is a great devotee and shares My own transcendental opulences. Thus, he is the right person for Me to send to Badarikāśrama. I shall give Uddhava complete transcendental knowledge by which one becomes detached from the material world, and he in turn can deliver this knowledge, the science of transcending the kingdom of illusion, to the worthy sages at Badarikāśrama. In this way he can teach them the method of rendering loving devotional service to My lotus feet. Such loving devotional service rendered to Me is the most valuable treasure, and by hearing such knowledge the desires of the great sages such as Nara-Nārāyaṇa will be completely fulfilled.

    “‘Those great souls who have surrendered unto Me are always equipped with transcendental knowledge and detachment from the material world. Sometimes, being busy in their devotional service, they may appear to forget Me. However, a pure devotee who has achieved the platform of love for Me will always be protected by such sincere devotion. Even if such a devotee should suddenly give up his life while neglecting to fix his mind intensely on Me, such a devotee’s loving feelings are so powerful that they afford him all protection. Even if there is a temporary moment of forgetfulness, such devotion will bring the devotee to My lotus feet, which are beyond the vision of ordinary, materialistic persons. Uddhava is My pure devotee. Knowledge of Me and detachment from this world have again been aroused in him because he can never give up My association.’”

    The sincere servants of Caitanya Mahāprabhu are vigorously endeavoring to spread this Kṛṣṇa consciousness movement for the pleasure of their spiritual master and Lord Kṛṣṇa. At the present time thousands of devotees in the Kṛṣṇa consciousness movement, in all parts of the world, are working long hours under difficult conditions to distribute transcendental literature and thus enlighten the general populace. In this effort the devotees have no personal motivation but are simply desirous of pleasing their spiritual master by distributing his books. The people who receive this literature usually have no previous experience of Kṛṣṇa consciousness, yet they are so impressed by the purity of the devotees they meet that they eagerly purchase the books and magazines. In order to execute the tremendous task of spreading Kṛṣṇa consciousness, the devotees are tirelessly laboring day and night because they are on the platform of loving devotion. Although superficially such busy devotees may occasionally not think directly of the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa, such loving devotion will undoubtedly take them back to Kṛṣṇa’s lotus feet, and being pleased by their service, the Lord Himself will again arouse their unflinching meditation upon His personal form. This is the beauty of bhakti-yoga, which depends wholly and solely on the mercy of the all-merciful Personality of Godhead, Śrī Kṛṣṇa. This is the only totally safe means of uprooting the deep desires for material enjoyment, attaining pure love for Kṛṣṇa and going beyond the material universe to the kingdom of God. As stated in Bhagavad-gītā (2.40) :

    nehābhikrama-nāśo ’sti pratyavāyo na vidyate sv-alpam apy asya dharmasya trāyate mahato bhayāt

    Lord Kṛṣṇa also advised Uddhava in this verse to give up the illusory attachment to so-called friends and family within this material world. One may not be able to physically give up association with family and friends, but one should understand that everyone and everything is part and parcel of God and is meant for the pleasure of God. As soon as one thinks, “This is my personal family,” immediately one will see the material world as no more than a place for enjoying family life. As soon as one is attached to one’s so-called family, false prestige and material possessiveness arise. Actually, everyone is part and parcel of God and therefore, on the spiritual platform, related to all other entities. This is called kṛṣṇa-sambandha, or the constitutional relationship with Kṛṣṇa. It is not possible to advance to the highest stage of spiritual awareness and at the same time maintain a petty material concept of society, friendship and love. One should experience all relationships on the higher, spiritual platform of kṛṣṇa-sambandha, which means seeing everything in relation to Lord Kṛṣṇa, the Personality of Godhead.

    One who is situated in his constitutional relationship with Kṛṣṇa can see all things in relation to Kṛṣṇa. He thus gives up the mundane urges of the body, mind and speech and travels throughout the earth as a devotee of the Lord. Such a highly elevated personality is called gosvāmī, or the master of the senses. This stage is described in Bhagavad-gītā (18.54) by the words brahma-bhūtaḥ prasannātmā: on the spiritual platform one attains complete satisfaction.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Now you should completely give up all attachment to your personal friends and relatives and fix your mind on me. Being always conscious of me, observing all things with equal vision, wander throughout the earth. The Lord thought within himself. I have fulfilled the desires of my devotees on earth who desired to see me, by going to places like Indraprastha and Mithila and thus killing Bāṇa and other demons, marrying Rukmiṇī, and meeting friends. I have shown myself to those on lower planets such as Bali and Yamarāja when I went there to retrieve the six sons of my guru. I have shown myself to Aditi and Kaśyapa in Svarga when I stole the pārijāta tree and to Mahāviṣṇu and others in Vaikuṇṭha when I went there to retrieve the son’s of the brāhmaṇa. But I have not fulfilled the longing of the great sages of Badrarikāśrama such as Nara-nārāyaṇa. And now the limit of my hundred and twenty-five years of manifested pastimes has expired. I should send Uddhava to Badarikāśrama since he is equal to me and is another form of myself. I will give him bhakti-yoga, like a valuable jewel, as a gift, along with jṣāna and vairāgya which are expressed by the term bhaga, in my name Bhagavān. Then their desires will be satisfied. Though Uddhava already has jṣāna and vairāgya arising from his full prema for me, and has no desire at the moment for separate teachings of jṣāna and vairāgya taught by me, I will produce a desire in him for this since this is my desire. Though he should actually die in sudden separation from me, I will preserve his life by my strong icchā-śakti and send him to that far off place. I will then establish him by my side, invisible to the material eye. Considering in this way, the Lord then imparted the desire for bhakti-yoga along with jṣāna and vairāgya in the heart of Uddhava. There are two types of affection for relatives and friends. One is affection for them based on one’s body, and the other is affection for them based on their relationship with me. It is possible to give up the first, and I will arrange that. But the second cannot be given up. “It is impossible for you to do so, and you will not be criticized.” Uddhava understood the Lord’s intention.

    Personal Guidance
    Give up clinging to "my people," fix the mind on Kṛṣṇa, and move through the world seeing every being and thing in relation to Him.
    Practical Applications
    • Name one relationship you label "mine" today and consciously re-offer that person to Kṛṣṇa as His, not yours.
    • Before leaving the house, fix the mind on Kṛṣṇa for two minutes so that errands, meetings and chance encounters are conducted on the platform of kṛṣṇa-sambandha.
    • When you meet a stranger today, refuse the usual sorting into useful/useless and instead see them as part and parcel of Kṛṣṇa.
    Reflection Questions
    • Which family or friend attachment am I quietly defending as "natural love" when it is actually the false prestige of "my people"?
    • Where does my so-called equal vision collapse — which kind of person can I still not see as part and parcel of Kṛṣṇa?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • Notice when your friend group or follower count is silently defining who you are, and offer that identity to Kṛṣṇa instead of feeding it another post.
    • Before an exam or interview, fix the mind on Kṛṣṇa for two minutes so that the result lands on the platform of kṛṣṇa-sambandha, not self-worth.
    • Speak to the classmate you usually overlook — the "useless" one — as part and parcel of Kṛṣṇa, not as someone outside your circle.
    householder
    • When making a family decision today — about money, schooling, or career — first ask how it serves Kṛṣṇa, then decide, refusing the trap of "this is just for my family."
    • Treat your children and spouse as souls entrusted to you by Kṛṣṇa rather than possessions of your own, and let one parenting choice today reflect that shift.
    • At work, perform your duties with equal vision toward colleagues, clients and competitors, seeing each as part and parcel of Kṛṣṇa rather than as instruments of your career.
    senior
    • Loosen one specific grip on a child, grandchild or old friend today by re-offering them to Kṛṣṇa, recognizing your time on this earth is being used up.
    • Use mentoring conversations to point others toward kṛṣṇa-sambandha rather than toward your own legacy or family name.
    • As the body declines, fix the mind on Kṛṣṇa during long stretches of the day so that, like Uddhava, you wander your remaining years with equal vision rather than nostalgia for "my people."
    Common Pitfalls
    • Mistaking emotional coldness or neglect of duties for the renunciation Kṛṣṇa asks of Uddhava here.
    • Reducing sama-dṛk to a vague "everyone is one" feeling, dropping the personalist anchor that the sameness is in relation to Kṛṣṇa.
    • Treating "wander throughout the earth" as license for restless travel or escapism rather than inner detachment while serving where one stands.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Share one relationship in which giving up snehaṁ sva-jana-bandhuṣu would be most painful for you, and what you suspect is hiding inside that pain.
    • Where in your life is "equal vision" actually indifference in disguise, and where is it genuinely seeing Kṛṣṇa in the other?
    • Kṛṣṇa tells Uddhava to wander the earth — what would it look like for a working householder to obey this verse without abandoning their post?
    Role Play

    A student has just received news that an aging parent is seriously ill back home. They come to you torn between flying back immediately out of family duty and staying to complete a service their guru has asked of them. Counsel them using this verse — neither flattening family obligation nor inflating it above kṛṣṇa-sambandha.

    Objections & Responses
    • Telling people to give up attachment to family sounds cold, even cruel — surely loving one's relatives is a virtue, not a bondage.
      Kṛṣṇa is not asking Uddhava to stop serving his relatives; He is asking him to stop seeing them as "mine" in isolation from Him. When the same person is seen as part and parcel of Kṛṣṇa, real care begins — care for their soul, not just their body — and false prestige and possessiveness fall away.
    • "Equal vision" sounds like the impersonal Brahman of the Advaitins — everything is one — which contradicts the personalist line you claim to follow.
      The purport is explicit: mayi here means paramātmani, and sama-dṛk means seeing Kṛṣṇa within everything and everything within Kṛṣṇa. The sameness is not an erasure of variety but a recognition that every variety stands in relation to the Supreme Person; mature knowledge of differences is preserved, not dissolved.

    Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam 11.7.7

    ↗
    యదిదం మనసా వాచా చక్షుర్భ్యాం శ్రవణాదిభి: । నశ్వరం గృహ్యమాణం చ విద్ధి మాయామనోమయమ్ ॥ ౭ ॥
    yad idaṁ manasā vācā
    [yad idam manasaa vaachaa]
    cakṣurbhyāṁ śravaṇādibhiḥ
    [chakshurbhyaam shravanaadibhih]

    [nashvaram grihyamaanam cha]

    [viddhi maayaa-mano-mayam]
    Word-for-word
    yat — that which idam — this world manasā — by the mind vācā — by speech cakṣurbhyām — by the eyes śravaṇa-ādibhiḥ — by the ears and other senses naśvaram — temporary gṛhyamāṇam — that which is being accepted or perceived ca — and viddhi — you should know māyā-manaḥ-mayam — it is only imagined to be real by the influence of māyā..

    My dear Uddhava, the material universe that you perceive through your mind, speech, eyes, ears and other senses is an illusory creation that one imagines to be real due to the influence of māyā. In fact, you should know that all of the objects of the material senses are temporary.
    Purport

    The question may be raised that since we find good and bad qualities throughout the material world, how can Lord Kṛṣṇa advise Uddhava to see everything equally? In this verse Kṛṣṇa explains that material good and evil are a creation of the illusory energy, just as the objects of a dream are a mental creation.

    As stated in Bhagavad-gītā, vāsudevaḥ sarvam iti: Lord Kṛṣṇa is actually everything because He is present within everything and everything is present within Him. Kṛṣṇa is sarva-loka-maheśvaram, the Lord and proprietor of all worlds. To see anything separate from Kṛṣṇa is illusion, and attraction to any kind of material illusion, either good or bad, is ultimately useless since it obliges the living entity to continue wandering in the cycle of birth and death.

    Seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching constitute the activities of the five knowledge-gathering senses. Similarly, the voice, the hands, the legs, the anus and the genitals constitute the five working senses. These ten senses are organized around the mind, which is the center of material activity. When the living entity desires to exploit matter, he is covered by the three modes of nature. Thus he concocts different philosophical, political and social explanations of reality but never understands the Absolute Truth, Lord Kṛṣṇa, who is beyond the contaminated perception of the material senses. One who is entangled in the network of material designations, such as race, nationality, sectarian religion, political affiliation, etc., is absorbed in the experience of combining his body and other bodies with material sense objects, thinking these sense objects to be sources of happiness and satisfaction. Unfortunately, the entire material world, along with the senses that experience it, is a temporary creation that will be annihilated by the time potency of the Supreme Lord. Despite our foolish hopes and dreams, there is no actual happiness on the material platform. The real truth is not material, nor is it temporary. The real truth is called ātmā, or the eternal soul, and among all eternal souls one is supreme. He is called the Personality of Godhead, and in His original form He is known as Kṛṣṇa. The knowledge-gathering process culminates in perception of the inconceivable, transcendental form of Kṛṣṇa. One who is not perceiving Kṛṣṇa in everything and everything in Kṛṣṇa is undoubtedly on the platform of mental concoction. In this verse Lord Kṛṣṇa warns Uddhava to remain clear of this illusory platform of existence.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    The material universe that you perceive through your mind, speech, eyes, ears and other senses is a temporary creation that is equivalent to what is made of māyā when you perceive in the waking state and to what is made of the mind when you perceive in the dream state. What is this seeing equally? That is explained in this verse. What you perceive by the mind and senses in the waking state is equivalent to what is made of māyā, and what you perceive in the dream state is equivalent to what is produced by the mind.

      His Holiness Mahavishnu Goswami· 2006-12-20· English
    • 2012-09-19 SB 11-07-07 - How one becomes entangled - Madhava Pr ISKCON Gainesville
      ISKCON Gainesville· 2012-09-19· English
    Personal Guidance
    What your mind and senses grasp as solid reality is māyā's temporary projection — see through it and locate Kṛṣṇa, who alone is real.
    Practical Applications
    • Pick one object you crave today — a purchase, a compliment, a meal — and trace it five years forward to its certain decay before acting on the craving.
    • When the mind insists "this situation is good" or "this is bad," pause and remember that both verdicts are sense-reports filtered through māyā, not the verse of reality.
    • Begin and end the day by speaking aloud "vāsudevaḥ sarvam iti" and naming three things in your immediate surroundings as Kṛṣṇa's energy, not standalone objects.
    Reflection Questions
    • Which one sense-object am I treating as a permanent source of happiness, and what will be left of it in twenty years?
    • Where in my life am I building philosophical, political, or social explanations of reality that quietly leave Kṛṣṇa out of the picture?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • Before posting or scrolling tonight, notice that every image on the feed is engineered to make a temporary sense-object feel like the source of your happiness — name it as māyā out loud before you tap.
    • When exam results, a crush's reply, or a friend group's approval feels like life-or-death, write down where that same feeling sat five years ago and what is left of it now.
    • Pick one peer you envy and one you pity, and look past the bodily situation to the same eternal soul in each — let that be the basis of how you speak to them this week.
    householder
    • When making a family financial decision today, ask explicitly: am I treating this house, school, or investment as permanent, and how does the answer change the choice?
    • In a disagreement with your spouse or child this week, pause when you feel "I am right, they are wrong" and remember both verdicts are sense-reports under māyā — then speak.
    • Bring Kṛṣṇa into one concrete daily act of family life — cooking, dropping kids at school, paying bills — by offering it aloud to Him, so the work stops feeling like an end in itself.
    senior
    • Walk through your home and identify three possessions you have quietly counted on as "yours forever" — name out loud the date by which each must be left behind.
    • When a body-pain or a diagnosis arrives, practice the dhīra-bhāva by addressing the body as a temporary instrument and Kṛṣṇa as the unchanging shelter, before reaching for the next distraction.
    • Identify one younger person this month and pass on, in your own plain words, the difference between material good-and-bad and the eternal soul — let your legacy be this discrimination, not your achievements.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Using "it's all māyā" to dismiss duties, relationships, and service — Kṛṣṇa calls the world illusory, not irrelevant.
    • Sliding into impersonal voidism — concluding that since objects are temporary, the truth must be formless, when the verse points to Kṛṣṇa, the personal Absolute behind everything.
    • Practicing intellectual detachment while remaining secretly attached — agreeing the senses deceive, yet still organizing the day around their pleasures.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Share one "good" thing in your life and one "bad" thing — then examine together how each is a māyā-construction your senses are reporting, and what changes when you say so out loud.
    • Where do members of the group disagree about what counts as "real life" — career, family, sādhana, social causes — and how does this verse force a re-ranking?
    • Discuss: if vāsudevaḥ sarvam iti is true, why does Kṛṣṇa still bother instructing Uddhava to discriminate between temporary and eternal? Is this a contradiction or a method?
    Role Play

    One student plays a friend who has just received a major promotion and a new house and is celebrating; the other plays a Gauḍīya practitioner who must congratulate sincerely without endorsing the illusion that these acquisitions are sources of lasting happiness — find words that honor the friendship without flattering māyā.

    Objections & Responses
    • If the world my senses report is illusory, this teaching is just escapism dressed up in Sanskrit — it lets me avoid suffering people and real problems.
      Kṛṣṇa is not telling Uddhava the world does not exist; He is saying the world's apparent independence from Him is the illusion. Real compassion begins by seeing the eternal soul inside the suffering body — that is engagement, not escape, and it goes deeper than any merely bodily relief.
    • Modern science confirms what my senses report — atoms, neurons, measurable phenomena. Calling all of this māyā is pre-scientific superstition.
      The verse does not deny that the senses report something; it denies that what they report is permanent or self-existing. Science itself agrees every measurable object is temporary and dependent. The further claim — that behind these temporary forms stands Kṛṣṇa, sarva-loka-maheśvaram — is what sādhana, not the microscope, is built to verify.

    Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam 11.7.8

    ↗

    One whose consciousness is bewildered by illusion perceives many differences in value and meaning among material objects. Thus one engages constantly on the platform of material good and evil and is bound by such conceptions. Absorbed in material duality, such a person contemplates the performance of compulsory duties, nonperformance of such duties and performance of forbidden activities.
    Purport

    The illusory mental platform of existence is described in this verse. The word ayuktasya indicates the conditioned soul who does not fix his mind on the Supreme Personality of Godhead. It is clearly described in Bhagavad-gītā and other Vedic literature that Lord Kṛṣṇa, the Absolute Truth, is within everything, and everything is within the Lord. The example may be given that when a woman loves a man, she is most eager to see him, and she daily sees him dressed in different clothes. Actually the woman is interested not in the clothes but in the man. Similarly, within every material object is the Supreme Personality of Godhead; therefore one who has developed love of God is constantly seeing the Lord everywhere, and not just the superficial material objects that cover the Lord.

    The word ayuktasya in this verse indicates one who has not come to the stage of reality. Such a person, being deprived of loving devotional service to Lord Kṛṣṇa, attempts to enjoy the innumerable forms and flavors of material experience. This temporary, illusory engagement is not the constitutional function of the bewildered living entity, who remains without any awareness of the ultimate reality, the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Within the world of matter there are undoubtedly varieties. Among dogs there are pedigree poodles and common mutts, and among horses there are thoroughbreds and old gray mares. Similarly, some human beings are beautiful and educated and others are dull and homely. Some are rich and some are poor. In nature we find fertile land and sterile land, lush forests and useless deserts, invaluable gems and colorless stones, flowing transparent rivers and stagnant dirty ponds. In human society we find happiness and distress, love and hate, victory and defeat, war and peace, life and death, and so on. However, we do not have any permanent relationship with any of these conditions, because we are eternal spirit souls, part and parcel of Lord Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Vedic culture is arranged in such a way that everyone can become perfect in self-realization simply by performing his occupational duty for the satisfaction of the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Sve sve karmaṇy abhirataḥ saṁsiddhiṁ labhate naraḥ. Some conditioned souls, however, believe that complete perfection in life may be achieved by performing ordinary, nonspiritual duties on behalf of family, nation, humanity, and so on. Others are interested in neither service to God nor noble mundane activities, and there are others who actively pursue sinful life. Such sinful persons generally rise from bed late in the afternoon and stay awake all night, taking intoxicants and engaging in illicit sex. Such a dark, hellish existence is caused by attraction to tamo-guṇa, the mode of ignorance. Actions in the mode of ignorance are called vikarma, as mentioned in this verse. Unfortunately, neither the materially responsible person nor the materially irresponsible person nor the sinful person can achieve the real perfection of life, Kṛṣṇa consciousness. Although different societies and different individuals maintain different concepts of good and evil, all material things are ultimately useless in terms of our eternal self-interest, which is Kṛṣṇa consciousness. This idea is expressed by the saintly King Citraketu in the Sixth Canto of Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam (6.17.20) :

    guṇa-pravāha etasmin kaḥ śāpaḥ ko nv anugrahaḥ kaḥ svargo narakaḥ ko vā kiṁ sukhaṁ duḥkham eva vā

    “This material world resembles the waves of a constantly flowing river. Therefore, what is a curse and what is a favor? What are the heavenly planets and what are the hellish planets? What is actually happiness and what is actually distress? Because the waves flow constantly, none of them has an eternal effect.” The argument may be given that since in the Vedas there are prescribed and forbidden activities, the Vedas also accept the concept of good and evil within the material world. The fact is, however, that it is not the Vedas themselves but the conditioned souls who are bound up in material duality. The function of Vedic literature is to engage each individual at the particular level on which he is presently situated and gradually elevate him to the perfection of life. The material mode of goodness is not itself spiritual, but it does not impede spiritual life. Since the material mode of goodness purifies one’s consciousness and creates a hankering for higher knowledge, it is a favorable platform from which to pursue spiritual life, just as the airport is a favorable place from which to travel. If a man desires to travel from New York to London, the New York airport is certainly the most favorable place from which to travel. But if the man misses his plane, he is no closer to London than anyone in New York who did not go to the airport. In other words, the advantage of the airport is meaningful only if one catches his plane. Similarly, the material mode of goodness is the most favorable situation from which to move up to the spiritual platform. The Vedas prescribe and forbid various activities to lift the conditioned soul to the material mode of goodness, and from that point he should rise to the spiritual platform by transcendental knowledge. Therefore if one does not come to the platform of Kṛṣṇa consciousness, his elevation to the material mode of goodness is useless, just as a trip to the airport is useless for one who misses his plane. In the Vedas there are injunctions and prohibitions that appear to accept good and evil among material things, but the ultimate purpose of the Vedic regulations is to create a favorable situation for spiritual life. If one can immediately take to spiritual life then there is no need to waste time with rituals within the modes of nature. Therefore Kṛṣṇa advises Arjuna in Bhagavad-gītā (2.45) :

    trai-guṇya-visayā vedā nistrai-guṇyo bhavārjuna nirdvandvo nitya-sattva-stho niryoga-kṣema ātmavān

    “The Vedas mainly deal with the subject of the three modes of material nature. Rise above these modes, O Arjuna. Be transcendental to all of them. Be free from all dualities and from all anxieties for gain and safety, and be established in the Self.” In this connection, Śrīla Madhvācārya has quoted the following verses from Mahābhārata:

    svargādyāś ca guṇāḥ sarve doṣāḥ sarve tathaiva ca ātmanaḥ kartṛtā-bhrāntyā jāyante nātra saṁśayaḥ

    “Within the material world, the conditioned souls consider residence on the heavenly planets and celestial pleasures, such as the pious enjoyment of beautiful women, to be good and desirable things. Similarly, painful or miserable conditions are considered to be evil or bad. However, all such perception of good and bad in the material world is undoubtedly based upon the fundamental mistake of considering oneself, and not the Supreme Personality of Godhead, to be the ultimate doer or performer of all actions.”

    paramātmānam evaikaṁ kartāraṁ vetti yaḥ pumān sa mucyate ’smāt saṁsārāt paramātmānam eti ca

    “On the other hand, a person who knows that the Supreme Personality of Godhead is the actual controller of material nature, and that it is ultimately He who is moving everything, can free himself from the bondage of material existence. Such a person goes to the abode of the Lord.”

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    An ignorant person perceives many illusory meanings with conceptions of good and bad. Thinking in terms of good and bad, the ignorant person sees differences in terms of prescribed actions, neglected actions and forbidden actions. This verse explains the previous verse. There are various meanings endowed with good or bad qualities. An ignorant person (ayuktasya) perceives erroneously. For persons who have fallen into the current of the guṇas, what is a good quality and what is a bad quality. What is a good object or bad object? Citraketu has said: guṇa-pravāha etasmin kaḥ śāpaḥ ko nv anugrahaḥ kaḥ svargo narakaḥ ko vā kiṁ sukhaṁ duḥkham eva vā In the river of the guṇas, what is a curse and what is a blessing, what is Svarga and hell, and what is happiness and sorrow? SB 6.17.20 “Are not good and bad expressed in the Vedas by injunctions and prohibitions?” Yes. But even the Vedas speak of this subject for the ignorant. Karma is prescribed actions. Akarma is neglect of those actions. Vikarma is prohibited action. These differences belong to a person who thinks in terms of good and bad, a person in ignorance.

    Personal Guidance
    Without fixing the mind on Kṛṣṇa, the soul drowns in material dualities of good and bad, duty and forbidden — only devotion ends the bewilderment.
    Practical Applications
    • Notice today when you label an event "good" or "bad" by bodily comfort alone, and re-evaluate it by whether it draws you toward or away from Kṛṣṇa.
    • Before any task, audibly state, "I am doing this as service to Kṛṣṇa," so the ayukta drift into mere karma, akarma, or vikarma is interrupted at the source.
    • Refuse to settle for the airport of sattva — at the end of the day, read or hear about Kṛṣṇa for fifteen minutes so the favorable platform actually carries you onward.
    Reflection Questions
    • Which dualities — praise/blame, gain/loss, success/failure — am I still treating as ultimate, and how has that bewilderment shaped this week's choices?
    • Where in my life am I sitting comfortably in the mode of goodness but missing the plane to the spiritual platform?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • When a grade, a follower count, or a rejection feels world-ending, name it aloud as guṇa-doṣa-dhī and ask whether it touches the soul at all.
    • Pick one "forbidden" habit your friend group treats as harmless — late nights, intoxicants, casual hookups — and recognize it specifically as vikarma rather than negotiable preference.
    • Choose your major, internship, or relationship this season by one extra criterion beyond prestige and pay: does it keep you near sādhana and devotee association, or pull you away?
    householder
    • When you and your spouse argue about a family decision, pause to ask which of the three — karma, akarma, vikarma — each option actually is, before debating preference.
    • Audit one recurring household expense or commitment that you justify as "responsible duty" and test whether it is moving the family toward Kṛṣṇa or merely polishing the airport.
    • Teach your children the categories of this verse in their own language this week — not as rules, but as a way to read their own school and friendship choices.
    senior
    • Review the last decade's hard-won judgments about who was good and who wronged you, and let this verse loosen at least one grudge you still carry as if it were eternal.
    • Decide concretely what of your estate, time, and attention will go toward Kṛṣṇa's service rather than only toward heirs and causes you consider noble.
    • When younger devotees come for counsel, resist giving advice purely in karma/akarma terms; show them the plane beyond the airport, drawing on your own near-misses.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Mistaking neutrality or tasteful living in sattva for actual Kṛṣṇa consciousness, and so never boarding the flight the purport describes.
    • Using "transcend duality" as license to abandon prescribed duties, collapsing the verse's three categories — karma, akarma, vikarma — into indifference.
    • Spiritualizing material preferences by calling whatever pleases the senses "Kṛṣṇa's arrangement" while quietly avoiding what is uncomfortable but devotional.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Share one situation this month where you were certain something was "bad" — has the verse's analysis of guṇa-doṣa-dhī changed your reading of it, or not?
    • The purport says the materially responsible person, the irresponsible person, and the sinful person all miss real perfection — which of these three is your most habitual disguise, and why?
    • Where do you and your partner or close devotee friends genuinely disagree about what counts as karma versus vikarma in daily life, and how do you resolve it?
    Role Play

    Two students pair up: one has just received a prestigious job offer that requires relocating away from association of devotees and a steady sādhana routine; the other plays a senior devotee. The first must defend the move using ordinary categories of duty and benefit; the second must apply this verse — ayukta perception, the airport-and-plane analogy, and the difference between sattva and Kṛṣṇa consciousness — without being preachy or dismissive.

    Objections & Responses
    • If good and evil are just bewildered dualities, isn't this verse basically moral relativism dressed in Sanskrit?
      The verse does not deny that some acts are karma, some akarma, and some vikarma — it explicitly names all three. What it denies is that material good and evil are ultimate. The Vedas still prescribe and prohibit, but as a ladder toward Kṛṣṇa, not as the final word. Relativism flattens the ladder; this verse points to what is above it.
    • I am a responsible professional supporting my family and giving in charity — calling that bewilderment seems insulting and impractical.
      Nothing here insults responsible work; Prabhupāda calls sattva the most favorable platform. The verse only warns that even the best material position is the airport, not London. Keep the responsibilities, but add the flight — hearing, chanting, and offering the day's work to Kṛṣṇa — so the favorable platform actually delivers you somewhere.

    Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam 11.7.9

    ↗
    తస్మాద్ యుక్తేన్ద్రియగ్రామో యుక్తచిత్త ఇదమ్ జగత్ । ఆత్మనీక్షస్వ వితతమాత్మానం మయ్యధీశ్వరే ॥ ౯ ॥
    tasmād yuktendriya-grāmo
    [tasmaad yuktendriya-graamo]
    yukta-citta idaṁ jagat
    [yukta-chitta idam jagat]
    ātmanīkṣasva vitatam
    [aatmaneekshasva vitatam]
    ātmānaṁ mayy adhīśvare
    [aatmaanam mayy adheeshvare]
    Word-for-word
    tasmāt — therefore yukta — having brought under control indriya-grāmaḥ — all the senses yukta — also subduing cittaḥ — your mind idam — this jagat — world ātmani — within the individual soul īkṣasva — you should see vitatam — spread out (as the substance of his material enjoyment) ātmānam — and that individual soul mayi — in Me adhīśvare — the supreme controller.
    Blended reading (Sanskrit + English inline)
    tasmād yuktendriya-grāmo

    yukta
    having brought under control
    indriya-grāmaḥ
    all the senses
    yukta-citta idaṁ jagat
    yukta
    also subduing
    cittaḥ

    idam
    this
    jagat

    ātmani
    within the individual soul
    īkṣasva
    you should see
    vitatam
