    mayi
    in Me
    adhīśvare
    the supreme controller.
    Therefore, bringing all your senses under control and thus subduing the mind, you should see the entire world as situated within the self, who is expanded everywhere, and you should also see this individual self within Me, the Supreme Personality of Godhead.
    Purport

    The word vitatam, or “widely expanded,” implies that the individual jīva soul is present throughout the material universe. Similarly, in Bhagavad-gītā (2.24) Lord Kṛṣṇa states, nityaḥ sarva-gataḥ: the individual soul is eternal and is expanded everywhere throughout the material and spiritual worlds. This does not mean, however, that each individual soul is all-pervading, but that the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Kṛṣṇa, has expanded His marginal potency everywhere. Thus, one should not blindly conclude that a minute living entity is all-pervading; rather, one should understand that God is great and expands His personal energy everywhere. In this verse, ātmanīkṣasva vitatam means that this material world is created to facilitate the sense gratification of the conditioned souls, who are trying to enjoy without Kṛṣṇa, their actual master. The living entities are busily trying to exploit the external energy of the Lord, but their jurisdiction over the material world is illusory. Both the material nature and the conditioned living being are energies of the Lord and thus exist within the Personality of Godhead and are under His supreme control.

    The individual living entity exists for the pleasure of the Personality of Godhead and is the Lord’s eternal servant. As soon as the senses become absorbed in material gratification they lose their power to experience the Absolute Truth. The actual goal of sense activity is satisfaction of Viṣṇu, the Lord, and all of the senses can experience infinite spiritual pleasure by perceiving and serving the Lord in His personal feature. Those who adopt the impersonal conception of God, however, try to stop all sense activity. But because the senses cannot remain permanently inactive they naturally return to activities in the realm of material illusion. If one engages the senses in the service of the Personality of Godhead, then one enjoys unlimited pleasure upon seeing the transcendental beauty of the Lord’s form. But unless one qualifies himself by pure loving devotion to Kṛṣṇa, the Lord does not award him this exalted experience. Therefore, every conditioned soul should end his unnecessary separation from the Personality of Godhead by rejoining the Lord’s blissful company. Lord Kṛṣṇa personally comes down to reopen the blind eyes of the conditioned souls, and thus the Lord is personally teaching Uddhava so that sincere souls in the future might take advantage of His instructions. Indeed, hundreds and millions of people even now derive spiritual enlightenment from Lord Kṛṣṇa’s instructions to Arjuna in Bhagavad-gītā.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Therefore, bringing all your senses under control and thus subduing the mind, you should see the entire world as the object of enjoyment for the jīvas, expanded everywhere, and you should also see the jīvas as controlled by me, Paramātmā. Controlling the senses and the mind, please see the world made of happiness and suffering as the object of enjoyment for the jīva (ātmani). And see that enjoyer, the jīva, situated in me as the controller, Paramātmā (adhīśvare).
    Related lectures
    • Tamohara Pr SB 11-07-09 - 2017-03-17 ISKCON Alachua
      His Grace Tamohara Prabhu· 2017-03-17· English
    Personal Guidance
    Rein in the senses and mind, see the whole world resting within the self, and see that self resting within Kṛṣṇa, the supreme controller.
    Practical Applications
    • Before each meal, pause and silently place the food, your senses, and the act of eating within Kṛṣṇa as the adhīśvara — the supreme controller.
    • Pick one sense that ran loose yesterday (eyes on a screen, tongue on gossip) and yoke it today by giving it Kṛṣṇa-related work instead of starving it.
    • When you next feel like the boss of your situation, name out loud one factor (weather, health, others" choices) that is plainly not yours to command, and offer that domain back to Him.
    Reflection Questions
    • In which corner of my life am I still pretending to be the īśvara, when the verse asks me to see myself situated within the adhīśvara?
    • When my senses are scattered, what specifically am I trying to enjoy apart from Kṛṣṇa — and what would it look like to bring that exact craving inside the picture this verse paints?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • Before opening social media, take ten seconds to place the phone, your eyes, and the next ten minutes within Kṛṣṇa as adhīśvara — then notice how the scroll feels different, or whether you still want to open it.
    • In your next group of friends, catch the moment your tongue is about to run loose on someone absent; yoke it instead to one honest, Kṛṣṇa-conscious thing you can say or to silence.
    • Before an exam or interview, drop the fantasy that you control the outcome — see the room, the panel, and your effort as situated within Him, and then do your work cleanly from there.
    householder
    • Walk through your home tonight and silently see each room — kitchen, children"s study, bedroom — as situated within Kṛṣṇa, not within your management; let one anxious grip in that house loosen as a result.
    • In the next family-money or career decision, name one variable you have been treating as fully yours to control (a child"s career path, a spouse"s health, a market move) and consciously hand that variable back to the adhīśvara before deciding.
    • Pick one sense-habit that is leaking the household"s energy (late-night screens, restaurant runs, idle phone calls) and re-yoke it this week to a concrete devotional use — reading, kīrtana with the family, serving prasāda.
    senior
    • Look at the body that has carried you through childhood, youth, and now this stage, and see it as situated within the self, and that self within Kṛṣṇa — let that double vision quiet one fear about aging or death today.
    • Identify one possession, role, or relationship you are still quietly holding as "mine to run" and, in plain words, offer its īśvara-ship back to Him; then mentor a younger person from that lighter place.
    • Choose one sense that has grown dull or one that still grasps (eyes for news, tongue for taste) and yoke it deliberately to Kṛṣṇa — daily reading aloud, regular prasāda discipline — so the indriya-grāma is handed over before the body is.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Reading "see the world within the self" in an impersonalist key, as if the jīva itself were all-pervading, instead of seeing the world resting in Kṛṣṇa"s expanded energy.
    • Treating sense-control as suppression and going numb, rather than re-routing the senses into the service of the Personality of Godhead.
    • Doing the meditation as a mental exercise while leaving daily sense habits untouched, so the vision never reaches the indriya-grāma the verse names first.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Share a recent moment when your senses were yukta (yoked) versus a moment when they were scattered — what concretely made the difference, and was Kṛṣṇa anywhere in the picture?
    • Prabhupāda warns against concluding that a minute living entity is all-pervading. Where have you heard this teaching collapsed into "I am everywhere" or "all is one," and what is lost when it is?
    • The verse moves in two steps: world-in-self, then self-in-Kṛṣṇa. Which step do you personally tend to skip, and what happens in your sādhana when you skip it?
    Role Play

    A senior devotee is mentoring a new student who has just read this verse and announces, "So I am the all-pervading self, and the world is inside me." Two students play the devotee and the new student; the devotee must correct the impersonalist drift using only the language of yukta-indriya-grāma, vitatam, and adhīśvara, without crushing the student"s enthusiasm. Other students observe and afterward name where the correction landed and where it missed.

    Objections & Responses
    • This sounds like standard mysticism — "see everything in the self" is in every tradition. Why dress it up in Sanskrit?
      The verse does not stop at "everything in the self." It explicitly places that self within Kṛṣṇa, the adhīśvare — the Supreme Personality of Godhead who controls both matter and the conditioned soul. Strip that second clause and you get a generic mysticism the verse itself refuses; keep it and you get a personal relationship with a specific Lord, which is the whole point.
    • Telling modern people to bring their senses under control just produces repression and burnout. Isn"t healthy enjoyment better than this austerity?
      Prabhupāda makes the same observation in the purport — impersonalists try to stop the senses, and the senses simply rebound into illusion. The verse is not asking for shutdown but for yukta senses: senses engaged in perceiving and serving Kṛṣṇa, where they finally taste the unlimited pleasure they were actually built for. That is the opposite of repression.

    • In the next family-money or career decision, name one variable you have been treating as fully yours to control (a child"s career path, a spouse"s health, a market move) and consciously hand that variable back to the adhīśvara before deciding.
    • Pick one sense-habit that is leaking the household"s energy (late-night screens, restaurant runs, idle phone calls) and re-yoke it this week to a concrete devotional use — reading, kīrtana with the family, serving prasāda.
    senior
    • Look at the body that has carried you through childhood, youth, and now this stage, and see it as situated within the self, and that self within Kṛṣṇa — let that double vision quiet one fear about aging or death today.
    • Identify one possession, role, or relationship you are still quietly holding as "mine to run" and, in plain words, offer its īśvara-ship back to Him; then mentor a younger person from that lighter place.
    • Choose one sense that has grown dull or one that still grasps (eyes for news, tongue for taste) and yoke it deliberately to Kṛṣṇa — daily reading aloud, regular prasāda discipline — so the indriya-grāma is handed over before the body is.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Reading "see the world within the self" in an impersonalist key, as if the jīva itself were all-pervading, instead of seeing the world resting in Kṛṣṇa"s expanded energy.
    • Treating sense-control as suppression and going numb, rather than re-routing the senses into the service of the Personality of Godhead.
    • Doing the meditation as a mental exercise while leaving daily sense habits untouched, so the vision never reaches the indriya-grāma the verse names first.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Share a recent moment when your senses were yukta (yoked) versus a moment when they were scattered — what concretely made the difference, and was Kṛṣṇa anywhere in the picture?
    • Prabhupāda warns against concluding that a minute living entity is all-pervading. Where have you heard this teaching collapsed into "I am everywhere" or "all is one," and what is lost when it is?
    • The verse moves in two steps: world-in-self, then self-in-Kṛṣṇa. Which step do you personally tend to skip, and what happens in your sādhana when you skip it?
    Role Play

    A senior devotee is mentoring a new student who has just read this verse and announces, "So I am the all-pervading self, and the world is inside me." Two students play the devotee and the new student; the devotee must correct the impersonalist drift using only the language of yukta-indriya-grāma, vitatam, and adhīśvara, without crushing the student"s enthusiasm. Other students observe and afterward name where the correction landed and where it missed.

    Objections & Responses
    • This sounds like standard mysticism — "see everything in the self" is in every tradition. Why dress it up in Sanskrit?
      The verse does not stop at "everything in the self." It explicitly places that self within Kṛṣṇa, the adhīśvare — the Supreme Personality of Godhead who controls both matter and the conditioned soul. Strip that second clause and you get a generic mysticism the verse itself refuses; keep it and you get a personal relationship with a specific Lord, which is the whole point.
    • Telling modern people to bring their senses under control just produces repression and burnout. Isn"t healthy enjoyment better than this austerity?
      Prabhupāda makes the same observation in the purport — impersonalists try to stop the senses, and the senses simply rebound into illusion. The verse is not asking for shutdown but for yukta senses: senses engaged in perceiving and serving Kṛṣṇa, where they finally taste the unlimited pleasure they were actually built for. That is the opposite of repression.
    📝 My note

    [jshaana-vijshaana-samyukta]

    Being fully endowed with conclusive knowledge of the Vedas and having realized the ultimate purpose of such knowledge in practice, you will be able to perceive the pure self, and thus your mind will be satisfied. At that time you will become dear to all living beings, headed by the demigods, and you will never be hampered by any disturbance in life.
    Purport

    As explained in Bhagavad-gītā, one whose mind is free from material desire becomes disinterested in demigod worship, since the purpose of such worship is material amelioration. The demigods, however, are never displeased with one who becomes a pure devotee of Lord Kṛṣṇa and offers all of his worship to the Lord. The demigods themselves are humble servants of Lord Kṛṣṇa, as was amply demonstrated in Lord Kṛṣṇa’s pastimes on the earth. One who can experience the eternal soul within everyone’s body certainly becomes dear to all living beings. Since he sees everyone as qualitatively equal to himself, he does not envy anyone nor try to lord it over any other living being. Being free from envy and a well-wisher of all, such a self-realized soul is naturally dear to everyone. As stated in the song to the Six Gosvāmīs, dhīrādhīra-jana-priyau priya-karau nirmatsarau pūjitau.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Being fully endowed with the conclusion of the Vedas and its realization, satisfied by realization of ātmā, being the object of affection by all beings, you will not be checked by any obstacles. “If one controls the mind and neglects to perform karmas, the devatās will create obstacles.” Being fixed in understanding the real meaning of the Vedas (jṣāna) and in realization of that meaning (vijṣāna), consequently being satisfied in your mind by realization of ātmā, and thus being the object of affection (ātmā-bhūtaḥ) by all beings, you will not be checked by obstacles. Śruti says tasya ha na devāś ca nābhūtyā īśate ātmā hy evaiṣāṁ sa bhavati: the devatās do not create obstacles for the person who has realized ātmā. (Bṛhad-āraṇyaka Upaniṣad1.4.10)
    Personal Guidance
    When jñāna ripens into vijñāna and you perceive the same soul in every body, envy dissolves, the mind rests, and no disturbance can derail you.
    Practical Applications
    • Before any interaction today, silently note: this person is an eternal soul, part of Kṛṣṇa — and then speak accordingly.
    • Stop mid-day and audit one place where you are still secretly trying to lord it over another living being, and renounce that posture.
    • When a disturbance lands — criticism, delay, bad news — refuse to be hampered; return immediately to chanting and the felt presence of the ātmā within.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where is my knowledge still only theoretical jñāna, not yet vijñāna lived in how I treat the person in front of me?
    • Which envies and rivalries reveal that I am not yet seeing the same soul in everyone, and what would it cost me to lay them down?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • In your friend group or class today, pick the person you most quietly compete with and do one small, unseen good turn for them — practice nirmatsara.
    • Before opening social media, remind yourself that every account is an eternal soul, not a metric — and refuse to compare your insides to their highlight reel.
    • When an exam result, a rejection, or a breakup lands hard, sit for ten minutes of japa instead of doom-scrolling, and let the disturbance not hamper your study or your sleep.
    householder
    • At the dinner table tonight, look at spouse and children as eternal souls entrusted to your care by Kṛṣṇa, and let that adjust your tone for the rest of the evening.
    • Audit one work decision this week where you are pursuing 'material amelioration' through subtle politics or one-upmanship, and re-do it as service rather than rivalry.
    • When the next family disturbance hits — a bill, an illness, a teenager's outburst — refuse to be hampered: keep your sādhana times non-negotiable that day.
    senior
    • Use your age as an asset for sama-darśana: in any room you now enter, deliberately see the youngest person there as the same eternal soul you are, and speak to them that way.
    • Loosen one attachment this month — a possession, a grievance, an old grudge — as concrete training in becoming nirmatsara before the body is taken.
    • When the body's disturbances multiply — pain, sleep, memory — practice nāntarāyair vihanyase by anchoring each day in ātma-anubhava through chanting, hearing, and mentoring at least one younger devotee.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Mistaking the verse for impersonal sama-darśana — collapsing Kṛṣṇa, demigods, and living beings into one undifferentiated Self instead of seeing souls qualitatively one with Him yet personally distinct.
    • Using ātma-anubhava as a license to withdraw from people, when the verse promises you will become dear to all living beings — engagement, not retreat.
    • Reading nāntarāyair vihanyase as a guarantee of a trouble-free life, rather than an inner steadiness that disturbance can no longer hamper.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Share one relationship where seeing the other as an eternal soul would force a concrete change in your behavior — and what is stopping you.
    • Where in your life does worship or effort still aim at material amelioration, and how would dropping that aim actually feel?
    • Tell the group about a recent 'disturbance' that hampered you, and discuss what specifically would have to be in place inside for it not to hamper you next time.
    Role Play

    A senior colleague has just publicly taken credit for work you did, in front of people whose opinion matters to your career. One student plays you, another the colleague; a third plays a fellow devotee you debrief with afterwards. Enact the moment of being passed over, then the debrief — practicing speaking and acting from ātma-anubhava: neither suppressing the situation, nor envying, nor surrendering your duty, while still seeing the same soul in the colleague.

    Objections & Responses
    • If a self-realized person is 'dear to all living beings,' why were saints like Prahlāda, Haridāsa Ṭhākura, and Mahāprabhu Himself persecuted? The verse looks empirically false.
      The verse describes the inner state of the realized soul and the response of beings to the degree they are themselves in sattva — demigods and pure-hearted persons are drawn to him. Envious materialists, covered by rajas and tamas, may still attack the body, but they cannot hamper the devotee's ātma-anubhava; Prahlāda is the textbook case of nāntarāyair vihanyase in the face of literal torture.
    • This sounds like spiritual bypassing — I should just 'perceive the pure self' and my mind will be satisfied, so I can ignore real injustice and my own legitimate needs.
      Notice the verse's first half: jñāna-vijñāna-saṁyukta — conclusive Vedic knowledge fully realized in practice. That practice includes sva-dharma, varṇāśrama, protecting the weak, and honest work. Seeing the soul in everyone does not cancel duty; it purifies the motive behind it from envy and lording-over to genuine well-wishing.

    Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam 11.7.11

    ↗
    దోషబుద్ధ్యోభయాతీతో నిషేధాన్న నివర్తతే । గుణబుద్ధ్యా చ విహితం న కరోతి యథార్భక: ॥ ౧౧ ॥
    doṣa-buddhyobhayātīto

    Word-for-word
    doṣa-buddhyā — because of thinking that such action is wrong ubhaya-atītaḥ — one who has transcended both (the conceptions of mundane right and wrong) niṣedhāt — from what is forbidden na nivartate — he does not desist guṇa-buddhyā — because of thinking it is good ca — also vihitam — what is enjoined na karoti — he does not do yathā — just like arbhakaḥ — a young child.

    One who has transcended material good and evil automatically acts in accordance with religious injunctions and avoids forbidden activities. The self-realized person does this spontaneously, like an innocent child, and not because he is thinking in terms of material good and evil.
    Purport

    One who has developed transcendental knowledge never acts whimsically. Śrīla Rūpa Gosvāmī describes two stages of devotional service: sādhana-bhakti and rāgānuga-bhakti. Rāgānuga-bhakti is the stage of spontaneous love of Godhead, whereas sādhana-bhakti means the conscientious practice of the regulative principles of devotional service. In most cases, one who is now enjoying transcendental consciousness has rigidly practiced the rules and regulations of devotional service. Thus, due to previous practice, one spontaneously avoids sinful life and acts in accordance with the standards of ordinary piety. This does not mean that a self-realized soul is consciously avoiding sin and pursuing piety. Rather, due to his self-realized nature, he spontaneously engages in the most exalted spiritual activities, just as an innocent child may spontaneously exhibit good qualities such as kindness, tolerance, and so on. The spiritual platform is called śuddha-sattva, or purified goodness, to distinguish it from the material mode of goodness, which is always to some extent polluted by the lower modes of passion and ignorance. Thus if a man in material goodness appears to be most pious in the eyes of the world, we can only imagine the spotless character of a self-realized soul in purified spiritual goodness. Therefore it is stated in Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam (5.18.12) :

    yasyāsti bhaktir bhagavaty akiṣcanā sarvair guṇais tatra samāsate surāḥ harāv abhaktasya kuto mahad-guṇā mano-rathenāsati dhāvato bahiḥ

    If one is a pure devotee of Lord Kṛṣṇa, he will automatically exhibit all the exalted qualities of the demigods. Such manifestation of purity is spontaneous, as explained in this verse.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    One who has transcended material good and evil automatically acts in accordance with religious injunctions and avoids forbidden activities. The self-realized person does this spontaneously, like an innocent child, and not because he is thinking in terms of material good and evil. One who has attained jṣāna acts as he pleases. The jṣānī who has surpassed thinking in terms of good and bad refrains from forbidden acts arising from of previous impressions of that nature, but without condemning such forbidden acts as bad. He generally engages in prescribed actions, but not thinking of them as good, just as an innocent child, devoid of conceptions of decisions and lack of decision, performs actions and refrains from certain acts.

    • Param Brahma Pr SB 11-07-11 - 2026-02-19 ISKCON Chicago
      His Grace Param Brahma Prabhu· 2026-02-19· English
    • DMS SB 11-07-11 - 2009-03-20
      His Holiness Devamrita Swami· 2009-03-20· English
    Personal Guidance
    The self-realized soul, having transcended material good and evil, spontaneously follows what is enjoined and avoids what is forbidden — like an innocent child, not by calculation.
    Practical Applications
    • Today, treat your rules of sādhana not as burdens to negotiate but as the soil in which spontaneous purity will one day grow.
    • Notice when you are weighing a forbidden act with calculation; refuse the calculation itself and lean instead on the regulative principle.
    • Offer one small act — chanting, eating, speaking — with childlike simplicity, without grading it as pious or impious.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where am I still performing piety as a transaction with material good and evil rather than letting it arise from purified consciousness?
    • Which regulative principle have I been bargaining with, and what would it look like to rigidly honor it until it becomes spontaneous?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • Pick one rule of your sādhana — early rising, no intoxication, japa rounds — and hold it rigidly for a semester, not negotiating with friends or moods.
    • Notice the calculation when peer pressure invites a forbidden act; refuse on principle, not on a case-by-case cost-benefit.
    • When you act kindly to a classmate, don't post it or replay it for credit — let the act stay unselfconscious, like a child's.
    householder
    • Establish family standards — meals, speech, screen use — as fixed regulative principles, so children inherit spontaneous piety rather than negotiated rules.
    • When a business decision tempts you with a borderline-forbidden shortcut, refuse without entering the calculation of 'how bad is it really.'
    • In daily duties toward spouse and children, drop the inner ledger of 'pious householder' and act from steady duty rather than self-image.
    senior
    • Let the regulative principles you have practiced for decades now mature into effortless habit, and stop tracking your own piety as a score.
    • Mentor younger devotees by modeling unselfconscious conduct, not by reciting your past austerities.
    • As mortality approaches, loosen the grip on being seen as 'good' and rest in śuddha-sattva — conduct offered to Kṛṣṇa, witnessed by Him alone.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Claiming the rāgānuga 'spontaneous' platform to justify skipping the rigorous sādhana that actually produces it.
    • Mistaking material sattva — refined, polite piety still mixed with rajas and tamas — for the śuddha-sattva this verse describes.
    • Imagining 'transcendence of good and evil' as license to act whimsically, when the verse defines it as effortless conformity to scripture.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Share an area where your obedience to a regulative principle still feels like calculation. What would make it effortless?
    • Where in your life do you see material goodness being mistaken — by you or others — for purified goodness?
    • Rūpa Gosvāmī's two stages: do you believe spontaneous bhakti can come without rigorous sādhana? Defend your view to a partner who disagrees.
    Role Play

    One student plays a serious sādhaka who has followed the four regulative principles strictly for years; the other plays a newer devotee who insists rules are unnecessary because 'pure devotees act spontaneously.' Argue the position from this verse and Prabhupāda's purport — that spontaneity is the fruit of disciplined practice, not its replacement.

    Objections & Responses
    • If a self-realized soul acts 'spontaneously,' isn't this just dressed-up moral intuition? Why bring Kṛṣṇa into it at all?
      Moral intuition in material consciousness is still colored by rajas and tamas — it shifts with culture, mood, and self-interest. The verse describes śuddha-sattva, purified goodness, which arises only when consciousness is fixed on Kṛṣṇa; the steadiness and universality of the resulting conduct is what distinguishes it from intuition.
    • The child analogy sounds naive — children are not actually moral, they are simply uninformed.
      Prabhupāda is not equating the devotee with a child's ignorance but with a child's unselfconsciousness. The self-realized soul does not calculate piety for reward, just as a kind child does not perform kindness for credit; the absence of egoic accounting, not the absence of knowledge, is the point.

    • Mentor younger devotees by modeling unselfconscious conduct, not by reciting your past austerities.
    • As mortality approaches, loosen the grip on being seen as 'good' and rest in śuddha-sattva — conduct offered to Kṛṣṇa, witnessed by Him alone.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Claiming the rāgānuga 'spontaneous' platform to justify skipping the rigorous sādhana that actually produces it.
    • Mistaking material sattva — refined, polite piety still mixed with rajas and tamas — for the śuddha-sattva this verse describes.
    • Imagining 'transcendence of good and evil' as license to act whimsically, when the verse defines it as effortless conformity to scripture.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Share an area where your obedience to a regulative principle still feels like calculation. What would make it effortless?
    • Where in your life do you see material goodness being mistaken — by you or others — for purified goodness?
    • Rūpa Gosvāmī's two stages: do you believe spontaneous bhakti can come without rigorous sādhana? Defend your view to a partner who disagrees.
    Role Play

    One student plays a serious sādhaka who has followed the four regulative principles strictly for years; the other plays a newer devotee who insists rules are unnecessary because 'pure devotees act spontaneously.' Argue the position from this verse and Prabhupāda's purport — that spontaneity is the fruit of disciplined practice, not its replacement.

    Objections & Responses
    • If a self-realized soul acts 'spontaneously,' isn't this just dressed-up moral intuition? Why bring Kṛṣṇa into it at all?
      Moral intuition in material consciousness is still colored by rajas and tamas — it shifts with culture, mood, and self-interest. The verse describes śuddha-sattva, purified goodness, which arises only when consciousness is fixed on Kṛṣṇa; the steadiness and universality of the resulting conduct is what distinguishes it from intuition.
    • The child analogy sounds naive — children are not actually moral, they are simply uninformed.
      Prabhupāda is not equating the devotee with a child's ignorance but with a child's unselfconsciousness. The self-realized soul does not calculate piety for reward, just as a kind child does not perform kindness for credit; the absence of egoic accounting, not the absence of knowledge, is the point.

    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    One who is the kind well-wisher of all living beings, who is peaceful and firmly fixed in knowledge and realization, sees me within all things. Such a person never again falls down into the cycle of birth and death.

      His Grace Balaram Shakti Prabhu· English

      His Grace Chaitanya Charan Prabhu· 2018-02-03· English
    • Param Brahma Pr SB 11-07-12-13 - 2026-02-20 ISKCON Chicago
      His Grace Param Brahma Prabhu· 2026-02-20· English
    • RGS SB 11-07-12-18 Hindi - Twenty-Four Guru-09
      His Holiness Radha Govinda Swami· English
    Personal Guidance
    Become the well-wisher of every being, peaceful and fixed in knowledge — see Kṛṣṇa within all, and the cycle of birth and death loses its grip.
    Practical Applications
    • Before each meeting today, silently wish the other's eternal welfare — not merely that they feel comfortable, but that they remember Kṛṣṇa.
    • When agitation rises, pause and recall that the same Kṛṣṇa within you dwells within the one provoking you, and respond from that recognition.
    • Spend ten minutes in silence reviewing the day through the lens of mad-ātmakaṁ viśvaṁ — where did you see Him, and where did you forget?
    Reflection Questions
    • Whom do I currently exclude from my circle of suhṛd — and what does that exclusion reveal about how partially I see Kṛṣṇa in all?
    • What unresolved disturbance keeps me from being śānta, and how is it tied to forgetting that everything rests within Him?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • In the next group chat argument, before replying, ask whether your words serve the other person's deeper good or just your status in the group.
    • Pick one classmate you quietly dislike and, for a week, pray for their genuine welfare — watch how your perception of them shifts.
    • When scrolling and comparison-anxiety hits, remind yourself that the same Kṛṣṇa within you is within everyone on the feed, and put the phone down.
    householder
    • In your next disagreement with your spouse, hold the recognition that Kṛṣṇa dwells in them — let that steady you before you speak.
    • When making a decision about your children's education or discipline, ask what serves their soul, not only what makes today smoother.
    • At work, identify one colleague you have been treating as an obstacle and begin acting as their suhṛd — without telling them, without expecting return.
    senior
    • Use the loosening of your social roles as an opportunity to widen your circle of suhṛd beyond family — pray for those you will never meet again.
    • When the body's diminishments arise, return to paśyan mad-ātmakaṁ viśvaṁ and let that vision steady you against fear of what is leaving.
    • Mentor a younger person not by giving advice they did not ask for, but by quietly wishing — and praying for — their eternal welfare.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Mistaking sentimental tolerance of bodily desires for being a suhṛd — real well-wishing serves the soul, not the body's preferences.
    • Treating 'seeing Kṛṣṇa in all' as an impersonalist merging into oneness, rather than recognizing Him as the personal Lord pervading and yet distinct.
    • Performing outward peacefulness while inwardly nursing grudges, mistaking suppression for the śānta-bhāva born of jṣāna-vijṣāna.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Share an instance where being a 'well-wisher' required you to disappoint someone materially — did you do it, or did you collapse into material compassion?
    • Where do you draw the line between śānta equanimity and passive avoidance of legitimate responsibility, and how do you tell them apart in yourself?
    • Discuss what changes in your behavior when you actually believe Kṛṣṇa is present in the person across from you — and what stays the same.
    Role Play

    A close family member announces a decision you believe will damage their spiritual life — a relationship, a career move, a habit. They ask for your blessing. Enact the conversation twice: first as a worldly well-wisher prioritizing their comfort, then as a suhṛd grounded in this verse who must speak truth without losing śānta-bhāva.

    Objections & Responses
    • Being a 'well-wisher of all beings' sounds like generic kindness — every religion teaches that. What is distinctive here?
      Generic kindness wishes the body well; the suhṛd of this verse wishes the soul well, which often requires actions the body resents. And the ground of that well-wishing is specific — seeing Kṛṣṇa within all, not a vague humanism. Without that vision, kindness eventually degrades into sentiment or fatigue.
    • If I see Kṛṣṇa in everyone, doesn't that dissolve the personal Lord into a pantheistic presence — basically impersonalism with a Sanskrit veneer?
      The verse says mad-ātmakaṁ viśvaṁ — the universe is resting in Him, not that He is reduced to the universe. He pervades as the Supersoul while remaining the personal Kṛṣṇa one surrenders to. Seeing Him within all sharpens the personalist relationship; it does not dissolve it.

    Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam 11.7.13

    ↗
    శ్రీశుక ఉవాచ ఇత్యాదిష్టో భగవతా మహాభాగవతో నృప । ఉద్ధవ: ప్రణిపత్యాహ తత్త్వంజిజ్ఞాసురచ్యుతమ్ ॥ ౧౩ ॥
    śrī-śuka uvāca
    [shree-shuka uvaacha]
    ity ādiṣṭo bhagavatā
    [ity aadishto bhagavataa]
    mahā-bhāgavato nṛpa
    [mahaa-bhaagavato nripa]
    uddhavaḥ praṇipatyāha
    [uddhavah pranipatyaaha]
    tattvaṁ jijṣāsur acyutam
    [tattvam jijshaasur achyutam]
    Word-for-word
    śrī-śukaḥ uvāca — Śrī Śukadeva Gosvāmī said iti — thus ādiṣṭaḥ — instructed bhagavatā — by the Supreme Lord mahā-bhāgavataḥ — the exalted devotee of the Lord nṛpa — O King uddhavaḥ — Uddhava praṇipatya — after bowing down to offer respects āha — spoke tattvam — the scientific truth jijṣāsuḥ — being eager to learn acyutam — unto the infallible Personality of Godhead.
    Blended reading (Sanskrit + English inline)
    śrī-śuka uvāca
    śrī-śukaḥ uvāca
    Śrī Śukadeva Gosvāmī said
    ity ādiṣṭo bhagavatā
    iti

    uddhavaḥ

    Śrī Śukadeva Gosvāmi said: O King, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Lord Kṛṣṇa, thus instructed His pure devotee Uddhava, who was eager to receive knowledge from the Lord. Uddhava then offered obeisances to the Lord and spoke as follows.
    Purport

    Uddhava is described here as tattvaṁ jijṣāsuḥ, or desiring to know the truth. It is clear from previous verses that Śrī Uddhava is a pure devotee of Lord Kṛṣṇa and that he considers devotional service to Lord Kṛṣṇa to be the perfection of life. Thus the words tattvaṁ jijṣāsuḥ indicate that since Lord Kṛṣṇa is about to leave the earth, Uddhava is most anxious to deepen his understanding of the Lord so that he may further advance in loving service at the Lord’s lotus feet. Unlike an ordinary philosopher or scholar, a pure devotee is not eager to acquire knowledge for personal gratification.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Śukadeva Gosvāmi said: O King! The Supreme Lord thus instructed his pure devotee Uddhava, who was eager to receive knowledge from the Lord. Uddhava then offered obeisances to the Lord and spoke as follows.
    Personal Guidance
    Like Uddhava, approach Kṛṣṇa with obeisances and an urgent inquiry into truth — not to collect knowledge, but to deepen loving service.
    Practical Applications
    • Before opening śāstra today, physically offer praṇāma and silently state you are inquiring to serve Kṛṣṇa better, not to impress anyone.
    • Identify one tattva (about Kṛṣṇa, the soul, or bhakti) that you have left half-understood, and bring a precise question on it to a senior devotee.
    • Refuse the scholar's posture of detached curiosity — read every verse as Uddhava did, knowing the Lord may withdraw at any moment.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where am I gathering spiritual information for personal gratification rather than as a tattva-jijñāsu eager to advance in service?
    • If I knew Kṛṣṇa were about to leave my life, what one question about Him would I urgently fall at His feet to ask?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • Before your next exam-prep session or scroll through social media, sit for two minutes and ask Kṛṣṇa one real question about your life — treat Him as a Person who hears, not as an idea.
    • Pick the friend or senior in your sanga who actually lives bhakti, and bring them one honest doubt this week instead of debating it with classmates online.
    • Refuse the campus pose of the cool skeptic who only asks questions to win arguments — practice Uddhava's posture of inquiring in order to serve, not to score points.
    householder
    • In the middle of your work and family obligations, carve out one short daily window where you inquire about Kṛṣṇa as a tattva-jijñāsu, not as a tired manager catching up on duties.
    • Bring one real question about dharma, money, or raising your children to a trusted senior Vaiṣṇava this month — frame it as Uddhava would, around how to serve Kṛṣṇa better in your āśrama.
    • Notice when you are 'researching' spirituality the way you research purchases — comparing options for personal benefit — and consciously shift into the mood of a servant approaching his Lord.
    senior
    • Acknowledge in your daily japa that your time, like Kṛṣṇa's earthly stay, is finite — and let that sharpen, not dull, your inquiry into Him.
    • Identify younger seekers in your family or community and model Uddhava's bhāva for them — show that even at your stage, you still bow and still ask.
    • Loosen attachment to being seen as the one with answers; let your remaining years be characterized by deeper questions about Kṛṣṇa rather than rehearsed conclusions.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Mistaking the accumulation of philosophical answers for the humble, service-oriented inquiry Uddhava models here.
    • Approaching guru and śāstra without praṇipāta — wanting the truth but unwilling to bow first.
    • Treating inquiry as optional once one already considers oneself a devotee, instead of intensifying it as bhakti matures.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Uddhava is already a mahā-bhāgavata, yet he still inquires — share with a partner where your own advancement has quietly turned into complacency about asking.
    • Compare the inquiry of an ordinary philosopher with that of a pure devotee — which one have you actually been practicing this past month, and what evidence shows it?
    • Discuss what it means concretely, in your daily life, to inquire acyutam — about the infallible Lord Himself — rather than about doctrine, ethics, or self-improvement.
    Role Play

    Two students pair up: one plays a sincere seeker who has read many books and prides himself on his knowledge; the other plays a senior devotee. The seeker approaches with a clever theological question. The senior devotee must redirect him into Uddhava's posture — first obeisances, then inquiry framed around deepening service to Kṛṣṇa before His departure — without shaming the seeker. Swap roles and try again.

    Objections & Responses
    • Asking questions is fine, but bowing down first feels theatrical and infantilizing — why can't I just inquire as an equal?
      The praṇipāta is not theatre; it is the diagnostic. Uddhava, a mahā-bhāgavata, still falls at Kṛṣṇa's feet because he knows tattva is not transferred between equals — it descends from one who has it to one who admits he does not. The bow is simply being honest about that asymmetry.
    • Isn't this kind of personal devotion to Kṛṣṇa just sentimental? Surely truth is impersonal and accessible by reason alone.
      Uddhava inquires of acyutam — the infallible Person — not of an abstract principle, and Kṛṣṇa Himself answers as a Person. The verse refuses the impersonal frame at the outset. Reason can clarify, but tattva about Kṛṣṇa is finally heard from Kṛṣṇa or from those who love Him, received in the posture of a servant.

    • Refuse the scholar's posture of detached curiosity — read every verse as Uddhava did, knowing the Lord may withdraw at any moment.

    ↗

    Śrī Uddhava said: My dear Lord, You alone award the results of yoga practice, and You are so kind that by Your own influence You distribute the perfection of yoga to Your devotee. Thus You are the Supreme Soul who is realized through yoga, and it is You who are the origin of all mystic power. For my supreme benefit You have explained the procedure for giving up the material world through the process of sannyāsa, or renunciation.
    Purport

    The word yogeśa here indicates that the Supreme Personality of Godhead awards the results of all yoga practices. Since all of the material and spiritual worlds emanate from the transcendental body of Kṛṣṇa, there is nothing to be achieved by any yoga process except Kṛṣṇa and His potencies. And since the Lord remains eternally the master of His potencies, no one can achieve anything through yoga, or any other spiritual or material process, except by the sanction of the Supreme Personality of Godhead. The word yoga means “linking up,” and unless we link ourselves with the Absolute Truth, we remain covered by the darkness of ignorance. Thus, Kṛṣṇa is the goal of yoga.

    In the material world we falsely try to link ourselves with the objects of the senses. Man wants to link with woman and woman with man, or one tries to link up with nationalism, socialism, capitalism or innumerable other creations of the illusory energy of the Lord. Since we are linking ourselves to temporary objects the relationships are temporary, the results are temporary, and at the time of death we become bewildered when all of our connections are suddenly cut off by māyā. If we link ourselves to Kṛṣṇa, however, our relationship with Him will continue even after death. As explained in Bhagavad-gītā, the relationship with Kṛṣṇa that we develop in this life will continue to increase in our next life until we achieve the supreme goal of entering Kṛṣṇa’s planet. Those who sincerely serve the mission of Caitanya Mahāprabhu, following the transcendental lifestyle prescribed by the Lord, will enter the Lord’s abode at the end of this lifetime.

    One can never achieve a permanent situation by mental speculation, and what to speak of by ordinary material sense gratification. By the methods of haṭha-yoga, karma-yoga, rāja-yoga, jṣāna-yoga, etc., one does not actually awaken his propensity for rendering eternal loving service to the Personality of Godhead. Thus, one is bereft of the transcendental tastes of spiritual enjoyment. Sometimes the conditioned soul, disgusted by his failure to gratify his senses, bitterly decides to renounce the material world and merge into an impersonal, painless transcendence. But our actual happy situation is to render loving service at the lotus feet of the Personality of Godhead. All of the different yoga processes gradually lead one to love of Godhead, and it is Lord Kṛṣṇa’s aim to reestablish the conditioned souls in this happy position. Caitanya Mahāprabhu is making this perfection easily available through the chanting of the holy name of Kṛṣṇa, the supreme yoga process for this age.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Uddhava said: O master of all types of yoga! O teacher of jṣāna-yoga! O embodiment of all yogas! O Lord, you make your appearance through bhakti-yoga! You have explained renunciation performed by sannyāsīs for the highest benefit. O master of yoga! O lord of the karma-yoga, jṣāna-yoga and bhakti-yoga! O presenter of jṣāna-yoga to me, who am not qualified for it! O personification of yoga! If I attain you, I have attained all yogas. However, since you appear through bhakti-yoga and appear within your devotees, you should particularly teach me bhakti-yoga.

    Personal Guidance
    Kṛṣṇa alone awards the fruit of yoga; true renunciation is linking everything back to Him, not merging into the impersonal.
    Practical Applications
    • Name one "link" you are currently leaning on for security — a relationship, a job title, a nation — and consciously re-offer that energy to Kṛṣṇa today.
    • Before any practice today (japa, study, work), say aloud that you are not the awarder of its result — Kṛṣṇa, the yogeśa, is.
    • Refuse to romanticize impersonal "merging" or stress-relief spirituality; choose one concrete act of loving service to Kṛṣṇa instead.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where am I quietly hoping yoga, study, or discipline will pay me out, rather than carry me to Kṛṣṇa Himself?
    • Which of my present "linkings" — to people, work, identity — will māyā cut at the moment of death, and what would it mean to begin loosening them now?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • Notice which identity you are currently "linking" yourself to — your college, your friend group, your follower count — and ask honestly what happens to you when that link is threatened.
    • Before your next exam, audition, or interview, formally tell Kṛṣṇa that He is the awarder of the result; then prepare harder, not less, because the effort is now an offering.
    • Refuse the campus pitch that meditation is just "self-care" for stress; try one round of chanting Kṛṣṇa's names today as a personal link, not a productivity hack.
    householder
    • Pick one decision this week — a job move, a school for the kids, a financial choice — and consciously make it as a trustee for Kṛṣṇa rather than as the proprietor of your family's future.
    • When you feel the urge to "escape" your responsibilities into a fantasy of retreat or simplicity, recognize it as material disgust, and instead re-link that day's work and relationships to Kṛṣṇa through a clear morning offering.
    • Lead one short kīrtana or reading at home this week so that your spouse and children see renunciation modeled not as withdrawal, but as a household linked to Kṛṣṇa.
    senior
    • Name three attachments you can begin to loosen now — a possession, a role, a grievance — and treat that loosening as practice for the moment when māyā will cut all links at death.
    • Stop measuring your legacy by what your children or students achieve materially, and start measuring it by how clearly you have pointed them toward Kṛṣṇa as the real yogeśa.
    • Make daily chanting of the holy name your central activity, trusting Caitanya Mahāprabhu's gift that this is the supreme yoga process for this age — and let lesser practices fall away without drama.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Treating sannyāsa or renunciation as merely walking away from responsibilities, instead of giving up false ownership and linking everything to Kṛṣṇa.
    • Practicing yoga or sādhana as a self-improvement project, forgetting that Kṛṣṇa, not technique, awards the result.
    • Mistaking the longing for an "impersonal, painless transcendence" for spiritual maturity, when it is actually disgust dressed up as detachment.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Share one "linking" in your life that feels permanent but is actually temporary — and what your honest resistance is to admitting that.
    • Uddhava asks the Lord to explain renunciation for his "supreme benefit." Where in your life are you asking the same question, and where are you avoiding asking it?
    • Is chanting the holy name really enough as the "supreme yoga process for this age," or do you secretly believe you need something more sophisticated? Be honest with your partner.
    Role Play

    One student plays a friend who has just quit their job, left their family situation, and announced they are "renouncing the world" to find inner peace through meditation and silence. The other student, drawing on this verse, must respond as a Gauḍīya friend — neither flattering the gesture nor mocking it, but distinguishing material disgust from real sannyāsa, and pointing toward linking with Kṛṣṇa rather than dissolving into the impersonal.

    Objections & Responses
    • Why does it matter whether I link to Kṛṣṇa personally? Surely any sincere spiritual practice — mindfulness, breathwork, even atheist ethics — produces the same calm and goodness.
      Calm and goodness are by-products, not the goal. This verse calls Kṛṣṇa yogeśa — the one who actually awards the fruit of any yoga. Impersonal practices may sedate the mind, but they do not awaken our eternal function: loving service to the Personality of Godhead. A temporary link gives a temporary result; an eternal link gives an eternal one.
    • Talk of "renunciation" and sannyāsa sounds escapist and irresponsible in the modern world — we have families, careers, and real problems to solve.
      Uddhava is not being told to abandon his duties; he is being shown how to give up false proprietorship. Real tyāga is not running from work, family, or society, but refusing to call them "mine" and instead offering them as service to Kṛṣṇa. That is more demanding than escape, not less — and it is exactly what Caitanya Mahāprabhu's line makes available through the holy name in the middle of ordinary life.

    My dear Lord, O Supreme Soul, for those whose minds are attached to sense gratification, and especially for those bereft of devotion unto You, such renunciation of material enjoyment is most difficult to perform. That is my opinion.
    Purport

    Those who are truly devoted to the Supreme Lord do not accept anything for their personal gratification but rather accept those things suitable to be offered in the Lord’s loving service. The word viṣayātmabhiḥ indicates those who desire material objects for their personal gratification instead of for the devotional service of the Lord. The minds of such materialistic persons are suitably disturbed, and it is virtually impossible for such persons to renounce material enjoyment. This is the opinion of Śrī Uddhava.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    O Lord! O Soul of all beings! For those whose minds are attached to sense enjoyment, and especially for those bereft of devotion unto you, such renunciation of material enjoyment is most difficult to perform. That is my opinion.
    Related lectures
    • Param Brahma Pr SB 11-07-15-16 - 2026-02-23 ISKCON Chicago
      His Grace Param Brahma Prabhu· 2026-02-23· English
    Personal Guidance
    For minds hooked on sense objects and bereft of devotion to Kṛṣṇa, renouncing material enjoyment is nearly impossible — bhakti is what makes tyāga doable.
    Practical Applications
    • Name one viṣaya you have been trying to ‘willpower' away — and today, instead, offer that same energy in some direct service to Kṛṣṇa.
    • Before any indulgence today, pause and ask: ‘Am I taking this for myself, or can I receive it as prasāda in His service?' — and act accordingly.
    • Refuse the modern script that renunciation is achieved through self-discipline alone; add one concrete bhakti act (japa, hearing, offering) to anchor every restraint.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where in my life have I been attempting tyāga as a viṣayātmā — gritting my teeth at the sense object — instead of through devotion to Kṛṣṇa?
    • What specific attachments have I quietly concluded are ‘too hard to give up,' and how would honest surrender to Him reframe their difficulty?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • Pick the one app or feed that owns your attention most, and instead of just deleting it, replace twenty of those minutes daily with hearing or chanting — let bhakti, not willpower, do the heavy lifting.
    • Before the next party, exam-week binge, or relationship drama, notice the viṣayātmā script running in your head and consciously hand that situation to Kṛṣṇa in a short prayer before you act.
    • When friends mock your attempts to cut back on something (drinking, gaming, gossip), do not defend it as self-improvement — name it as a small step in devotion, and let that honesty filter your circle.
    householder
    • Identify one family expense or lifestyle upgrade you have been chasing for personal gratification, and reframe the decision by asking how it serves your family's actual sādhana, not just your comfort.
    • Build a non-negotiable household bhakti anchor (morning japa, evening Bhāgavatam reading, Sunday offering) so the renunciations you and your spouse make in money, time, and food are supported by devotion, not white-knuckled.
    • When parenting, stop trying to make your children renounce screens, sweets, or status purely by rules — model and invite them into devotional alternatives that genuinely compete for their hearts.
    senior
    • Take one possession, role, or identity you have been gripping (a title, a property, a way of being needed) and, in concrete steps this month, begin offering it into Kṛṣṇa's service rather than waiting for circumstances to pry it loose.
    • Use the natural loosening that age brings — reduced appetite, smaller social world, slowing body — as raw material for genuine vairāgya by tying each diminishment to increased hearing, chanting, and remembrance.
    • Mentor a younger person not by lecturing them on what to give up, but by sharing honestly where your own non-devotional renunciations failed and where devotion finally made tyāga real.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Treating Uddhava's words as license to give up on renunciation — ‘it's impossible without bhakti, so why try' — instead of as a call to deepen devotion.
    • Mistaking dry, willpower-driven suppression of desires for tyāga, and then collapsing into rebound indulgence when the strain breaks.
    • Assuming ‘being a devotee' automatically makes renunciation easy, without doing the actual sādhana that loosens the grip of viṣaya on the mind.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Share one area where you have tried to renounce something without devotional support — what actually happened, and what does this verse reveal about that experience?
    • Uddhava says this renunciation is ‘most difficult' for the viṣayātmā — do we agree that devotion makes it easier, or does it sometimes make giving things up harder before it gets easier?
    • When a friend who is not a devotee tries to renounce a bad habit, how do we honor their effort while honestly holding the view that bhakti is the real basis of tyāga?
    Role Play

    Two students sit together: one has just decided to quit social media ‘cold turkey' through pure willpower and is already irritable on day three; the other is a devotee who has been reducing the same habit by replacing scrolling time with hearing from the Bhāgavatam. The devotee must, in this verse's spirit, neither moralize nor flatter — but help the friend see why tyāga without bhakti is so brittle, and offer one practical bhakti-anchored step the friend can actually take.

    Objections & Responses
    • Plenty of non-devotees — Stoics, monks of other paths, even disciplined atheists — successfully renounce sense pleasures. So Uddhava's claim that it is ‘virtually impossible' without devotion to Kṛṣṇa is just sectarian overreach.
      Outward restraint is not the same as tyāga of the kāma in the mind. The Gītā (2.59) notes that the rasa, the inner taste, only leaves on seeing the Supreme. Others may discipline the senses heroically, yet the appetite often returns under stress, or migrates to subtler objects — pride, control, reputation. Uddhava is speaking of that deep, rooted renunciation where the mind itself loses its pull toward viṣaya, and in the Gauḍīya line that comes through loving attachment to Kṛṣṇa, not against Him.
    • If renunciation is ‘most difficult' for ordinary people like me, this verse just sets an impossibly high bar and breeds despair — it sounds like the tradition is telling householders to give up before they start.
      Read it the other way: Uddhava is being honest precisely so we stop blaming ourselves for the wrong thing. The verse does not say ‘try harder at renunciation'; it diagnoses why brute-force tyāga keeps failing and points us toward bhakti as the practical solution. For a householder, that means not abandoning duties but converting them — earning, cooking, parenting, working — into offerings to Kṛṣṇa, so detachment grows organically as attachment to Him grows.

    • Share one area where you have tried to renounce something without devotional support — what actually happened, and what does this verse reveal about that experience?
    • Uddhava says this renunciation is ‘most difficult' for the viṣayātmā — do we agree that devotion makes it easier, or does it sometimes make giving things up harder before it gets easier?
    • When a friend who is not a devotee tries to renounce a bad habit, how do we honor their effort while honestly holding the view that bhakti is the real basis of tyāga?
    Role Play

    Two students sit together: one has just decided to quit social media ‘cold turkey' through pure willpower and is already irritable on day three; the other is a devotee who has been reducing the same habit by replacing scrolling time with hearing from the Bhāgavatam. The devotee must, in this verse's spirit, neither moralize nor flatter — but help the friend see why tyāga without bhakti is so brittle, and offer one practical bhakti-anchored step the friend can actually take.

    Objections & Responses
    • Plenty of non-devotees — Stoics, monks of other paths, even disciplined atheists — successfully renounce sense pleasures. So Uddhava's claim that it is ‘virtually impossible' without devotion to Kṛṣṇa is just sectarian overreach.
      Outward restraint is not the same as tyāga of the kāma in the mind. The Gītā (2.59) notes that the rasa, the inner taste, only leaves on seeing the Supreme. Others may discipline the senses heroically, yet the appetite often returns under stress, or migrates to subtler objects — pride, control, reputation. Uddhava is speaking of that deep, rooted renunciation where the mind itself loses its pull toward viṣaya, and in the Gauḍīya line that comes through loving attachment to Kṛṣṇa, not against Him.
    • If renunciation is ‘most difficult' for ordinary people like me, this verse just sets an impossibly high bar and breeds despair — it sounds like the tradition is telling householders to give up before they start.
      Read it the other way: Uddhava is being honest precisely so we stop blaming ourselves for the wrong thing. The verse does not say ‘try harder at renunciation'; it diagnoses why brute-force tyāga keeps failing and points us toward bhakti as the practical solution. For a householder, that means not abandoning duties but converting them — earning, cooking, parenting, working — into offerings to Kṛṣṇa, so detachment grows organically as attachment to Him grows.

    O my Lord, I myself am most foolish because my consciousness is merged in the material body and bodily relations, which are all manufactured by Your illusory energy. Thus I am thinking, “I am this body, and all of these relatives are mine.” Therefore, my Lord, please instruct Your poor servant. Please tell me how I can very easily carry out Your instructions.
    Purport

    It is very difficult to give up false identification with the material body, and thus we remain attached to our so-called bodily relations such as wife, children, friends, and so on. Bodily attachment causes intense pain within the heart, and we are stunned by lamentation and hankering. Śrī Uddhava, a pure devotee of the Lord, here speaks like an ordinary person showing how to pray to the Personality of Godhead. We practically see that many sinful persons enter the International Society for Krishna Consciousness and after preliminary purification become most repentant for their previous illicit activities. They are shocked when they realize how they gave up the personal association of God to pursue the useless forms created by māyā; therefore they wholeheartedly pray to the spiritual master and Lord Kṛṣṇa to be engaged eternally in transcendental devotional service. Such a repentant, eager mentality is most auspicious for spiritual advancement. The Lord certainly answers the prayers of a repentant devotee desperate to escape the clutches of illusion.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    O Lord! A fool, I am deeply absorbed in the concept of I and mine related to the body and its corollaries produced by your māyā. Please instruct me, your servant, so that I can easily accomplish the jṣāna you have just explained. I am absorbed in material enjoyment because I am deeply involved with sons and wife related to my body created by your māyā. I identify with the blind well of the body. Teach me how to give up that absorption and deliver me. Teach me first the actions and then teach about jṣāna.
    Related lectures
    • Navina Nirada Pr SB 11-07-16 - A Devotee is unhappy to see others unhappy - 2009-03-24 ISKCON Melbourne
      Book distribution· 2009-03-24· English
    Personal Guidance
    Uddhava confesses that bodily "I and mine" thinking is māyā's net, and begs Kṛṣṇa to instruct him simply enough that he can actually carry it out.
    Practical Applications
    • Notice each time today the phrase "mine" arises about body, family, or status, and silently re-label it as Kṛṣṇa's property held in trust.
    • Before any decision, pray in Uddhava's tone: "I am foolish, please instruct Your servant," and only then act on the next obvious duty.
    • Refuse the modern story that you are your résumé and relationships; speak of yourself today as an eternal servant of Kṛṣṇa first, role-holder second.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where am I still calling "mine" something that Kṛṣṇa's māyā merely loaned to this body, and what would change in my conduct if I admitted it?
    • Am I willing, like Uddhava, to call myself foolish in front of the Lord and ask for instruction I can actually execute, rather than instruction that flatters me?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • When your phone shows likes, grades, or rejections, pause and notice the thought "this is me" — then re-say internally, "this is just the body's situation, I am Kṛṣṇa's servant."
    • Pick one area where you secretly feel foolish — a class, a friendship, a habit — and bring it honestly to Kṛṣṇa or a trusted senior devotee, asking for one doable instruction rather than hiding it.
    • Refuse the campus pressure to brand yourself by family, college, or relationship status; in at least one conversation this week, let your identity as a servant of Kṛṣṇa quietly come first.
    householder
    • In the next family or money decision, before reacting, silently pray Uddhava's words and ask what a servant of Kṛṣṇa, not an owner, would do here.
    • Speak with your spouse this week about one area where "mine" — my career, my kids' achievements, my home — has been driving you, and renegotiate it as a shared service to Kṛṣṇa.
    • Choose one concrete, easily executable instruction from guru and śāstra (a fixed chanting time, an offering before meals, a weekly association) and lock it into the household schedule as non-negotiable.
    senior
    • As you watch the body age, repeat Uddhava's confession daily and let each new limitation loosen, not tighten, your grip on "I and mine."
    • Review your will, possessions, and remaining responsibilities as a steward returning Kṛṣṇa's property, and make at least one concrete handover this season to reduce attachment.
    • When a younger family member or seeker approaches in confusion, refuse the role of proprietor-patriarch and instead model Uddhava's mood: confess your own dependence on Kṛṣṇa and point them to instruction they can actually carry out.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Confessing foolishness verbally while quietly continuing to manage life as the proprietor of body, spouse, and children.
    • Treating "all relations are māyā" as license to neglect dependents, instead of as a call to serve them as souls entrusted by Kṛṣṇa.
    • Waiting for an exotic revelation while ignoring the simple, already-given instructions of guru, śāstra, and sādhus that one is competent to follow today.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Share one specific relationship in which you most strongly feel "this is mine" — is that bond an obstacle, a service, or both, and how do you tell?
    • Uddhava asks for instruction he can easily carry out. What instruction have you already received that you keep postponing because it feels too small or too hard?
    • What is the difference, in your own life, between healthy responsibility for family and the ahaṅkāra of ownership Uddhava is repenting of here?
    Role Play

    One student plays a sincere newcomer who has just realized that years of identifying with career and family were rooted in bodily ego; they approach a second student, playing a senior devotee, and ask, in Uddhava's mood, for one simple instruction they can begin executing tomorrow morning. The senior devotee must respond without abstractions, giving a concrete sādhana the newcomer can actually do, while honoring their existing obligations.

    Objections & Responses
    • Calling love for my spouse and children an illusion manufactured by māyā sounds cold and even cruel; surely these bonds are the best part of being human.
      Uddhava is not denying that the relationships exist or that they involve real feeling; he is naming the false conviction that these bodies are the persons and that they belong to him. When you see your spouse and children as eternal souls placed in your care by Kṛṣṇa, your affection deepens rather than dies, because it is no longer doomed to end at the next bodily transition.
    • Why should a self-respecting modern adult stand before any God and call himself foolish and a servant? That seems like exactly the religious self-abasement we have outgrown.
      Uddhava is one of Kṛṣṇa's most exalted associates, and yet he speaks this way — not from low self-esteem but from accurate self-knowledge in the presence of the Supreme Person. To insist on being one's own master while being tossed by birth, disease, old age, and death is the real indignity; admitting servanthood to Kṛṣṇa is the moment a person first stands at full height.

    Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam 11.7.17

    ↗
    సత్యస్య తే స్వద‍ృశ ఆత్మన ఆత్మనోఽన్యం వక్తారమీశ విబుధేష్వపి నానుచక్షే । సర్వే విమోహితధియస్తవ మాయయేమే బ్రహ్మాదయస్తనుభృతో బహిరర్థభావా: ॥ ౧౭ ॥

    My dear Lord, You are the Absolute Truth, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, and You reveal Yourself to Your devotees. Besides Your Lordship, I do not see anyone who can actually explain perfect knowledge to me. Such a perfect teacher is not to be found even among the demigods in heaven. Indeed, all of the demigods, headed by Lord Brahmā, are bewildered by Your illusory potency. They are conditioned souls who accept their own material bodies and bodily expansions to be the highest truth.
    Purport

    All conditioned souls, from Lord Brahmā down to the insignificant ant, are declared by Śrī Uddhava to be covered by material bodies produced by the illusory potency of the Lord. The demigods in heaven, being absorbed in universal management, constantly utilize their fabulous material potencies. They therefore gradually fix their minds upon their mystically empowered bodies and also upon their bodily expansions such as their celestial wives, children, co-workers and friends. In the course of life in the heavenly planets, the demigods become conditioned to think in terms of material good and bad, and thus they accept the immediate welfare of their bodies to be the highest goal of life.

    The demigods do, however, try to strictly follow the laws of God. And to help them do this, the Supreme Lord descends to remind the heavenly beings of His own supreme personality, which possesses powers infinitely exceeding theirs. Lord Viṣṇu has an eternal body, full of bliss, knowledge and unlimited variegated potencies, whereas the demigods possess only deluxe material forms, subject to birth, death, old age and disease.

    Because the demigods are attached to ruling the created universe, their devotion to God is tinged with material desires. They are therefore attracted to those portions of Vedic knowledge that award the various material opulences necessary for perpetuating their celestial life. Śrī Uddhava, however, being a pure devotee of the Lord, is determined to go back home, back to Godhead, for eternal life and is thus not at all interested in the sophisticated Vedic knowledge of the demigods. The material world is a gigantic prison, whose inmates are subjected to birth, death, old age and illusion, and a pure devotee has no desire to remain there even as a first-class prisoner, like the demigods. Śrī Uddhava desires to return to the kingdom of God and for this reason directly approaches the Personality of Godhead. The Lord is sva-dṛśaḥ, or one who reveals Himself to His devotee. Thus, only the Lord Himself or His pure devotee, who faithfully repeats the Lord’s message, can take one beyond the material sky into the free atmosphere of the spiritual planets, where the liberated souls enjoy an eternal life of bliss and omniscience.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    O Lord! Among all the lords, I do not see anyone except you-- who give benefit to your devotees, who know me, and who can explain this to me, since you are Paramātmā. Brahmā and others, embodied beings, thinking in terms of the external world, are all bewildered by your māyā. The genitive case for satyasya and other words instead of the ablative is poetic license. I see no one other than you, who are the cause of al existence in time and space, or who gives benefit to the devotees (satyasya),who have knowledge of me (sva-dṛśaḥ), and who can speak to me, since you are the Paramātmā different from me(ātmanaḥ anyam).
    Related lectures
    • RCP SB 11-07-17 Telugu - 2015-12-12 ISKCON Tirupati
      His Grace Rupeshwar Caitanya Prabhu· 2015-12-12· Telugu
    Personal Guidance
    Only Kṛṣṇa, who reveals Himself to His devotees, can give perfect knowledge — even Brahmā and the demigods are bewildered by māyā into body-identification.
    Practical Applications
    • Before opening any teaching today, pray briefly to Kṛṣṇa as sva-dṛśa — the one who reveals Himself — rather than relying only on your own intellect.
    • Notice when you reach for a high-status human authority (academic, celebrity, demigod-like figure) to settle a spiritual question, and instead test the answer against Kṛṣṇa's words and a pure devotee's.
    • Refuse to treat your body, your spouse, your children, or your work as the highest truth this evening — name each one aloud as belonging to Kṛṣṇa before sleep.
    Reflection Questions
    • Whose voice — which teacher, expert, or celestial figure — have I been quietly trusting more than Kṛṣṇa's own self-disclosure, and why?
    • In which corner of my life am I, like Brahmā in this verse, mistaking my powers, roles, and bodily expansions for the highest truth?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • Before your next exam or interview, take thirty seconds to remember that the professor, recruiter, or top-ranked influencer is, in this verse's terms, also a conditioned soul — useful, but not the source of perfect knowledge.
    • Pick one account you follow obsessively on social media and ask honestly: am I treating this person like a demigod whose body, lifestyle, and opinions define what is real?
    • When friends pressure you toward a path because "everyone smart agrees," pause and bring the question instead to śāstra and one trusted devotee, the way Uddhava brought his question directly to Kṛṣṇa.
    householder
    • In your next big family decision — school, job change, money, move — explicitly name your spouse, children, and assets as belonging to Kṛṣṇa before you weigh options, so you do not silently treat bahir-artha as the highest good.
    • Audit which voices most shape your parenting and career — bosses, in-laws, parenting experts — and consciously place Kṛṣṇa's instructions and a pure devotee's guidance above them, without becoming rude or rebellious.
    • When stress tells you "my body, my family, my position must be protected at all costs," recognize this as the same vimohita-dhī Uddhava describes in the demigods, and respond by chanting and serving rather than scheming.
    senior
    • Notice where you still introduce yourself by past titles, achievements, or family roles, and practice instead seeing yourself as Kṛṣṇa's eternal servant, not your bodily expansions.
    • Choose one younger person to mentor not toward worldly success but toward direct dependence on Kṛṣṇa and śāstra, modeling Uddhava's posture of going to the source.
    • As health and friends fade, refuse the demigod-style strategy of clinging to deluxe material arrangements; instead, deepen daily hearing and chanting so that, like Uddhava, you are oriented toward going back to Godhead.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Reading this verse as license to dismiss śāstra and guru, when Uddhava is precisely modeling how to approach Kṛṣṇa through humble inquiry, not lone seeking.
    • Hearing "even Brahmā is bewildered" and concluding all teachers are equally deluded, instead of recognizing the pure devotee who faithfully repeats Kṛṣṇa's message as the trustworthy channel.
    • Treating bahir-artha-bhāva (taking external things as the goal) as a problem only for kings and celebrities, while ignoring one's own quieter worship of career, family image, and bodily comfort.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Uddhava says he sees no qualified teacher even among the demigods — where in your own life do you keep searching horizontally among peers and experts for an answer this verse says is only available vertically, from Kṛṣṇa?
    • What is the practical difference between honoring varṇāśrama authorities (parents, teachers, elders) and treating them as final givers of perfect knowledge — and where in your week do you blur the two?
    • If even Brahmā is described as vimohita-dhī, bewildered in intelligence, what should that do to our confidence in our own conclusions about meaning, success, and death?
    Role Play

    One student plays a sincere seeker who has just been offered a prestigious spiritual teaching post by a famous non-devotee guru with massive following and clear material results; the other plays a senior Gauḍīya friend. Using SB 11.7.17, the friend must help the seeker see why even an apparently powerful, demigod-like teacher is not sufficient, without becoming dismissive, arrogant, or sectarian.

    Objections & Responses
    • Saying only Kṛṣṇa can give perfect knowledge sounds arrogant and exclusivist — surely sincere teachers in every tradition, and even brilliant secular thinkers, also have real insight.
      Uddhava is not denying that demigods and great souls have partial knowledge — he explicitly addresses Brahmā and the demigods with respect. He is saying that perfect knowledge of the Absolute Truth must come from the Absolute Truth Himself, because anyone still identified with a material body, however refined, is by definition reading reality from inside the illusion. That is not arrogance; it is a structural point about who is positioned to see the whole.
    • This sounds like blind faith — I am supposed to trust an invisible Kṛṣṇa over visible, testable human authorities?
      Kṛṣṇa is called sva-dṛśa precisely because He reveals Himself — through śāstra, through the disciplic line, and through the pure devotee who faithfully repeats His message. We are not asked to bypass evidence; we are asked to weigh visible human authorities against this self-revealing source, the same way Uddhava, a learned and worldly man, ultimately did.
