    A saintly person should learn from the mountain to devote all his efforts to the service of others and to make the welfare of others the sole reason for his existence. Similarly, as the disciple of the tree, he should learn to dedicate himself to others.
    Purport

    Great mountains bear unlimited quantities of earth, which in turn give sustenance to innumerable forms of life such as trees, grass, birds, animals, and so on. Mountains also pour forth unlimited quantities of crystalline water in the form of waterfalls and rivers, and this water gives life to all. By studying the example of mountains, one should learn the art of providing for the happiness of all living entities. Similarly, one may take excellent lessons from the pious trees, who offer innumerable benefits, such as fruits, flowers, cooling shade and medicinal extracts. Even when a tree is suddenly cut down and dragged away, the tree does not protest but continues to give service to others in the form of firewood. Thus, one should become the disciple of such magnanimous trees and learn from them the qualities of saintly conduct.

    According to Śrīla Madhvācārya, the word parārthaikānta-sambhavaḥ indicates that one should dedicate all of one’s wealth and other assets to the welfare of others. By one’s acquired opulence, one should especially try to please the spiritual master and the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Thus, the demigods, as well as all truly respectable superior personalities, will automatically be pleased. By developing saintly conduct, as described in this verse, one will become tolerant, and this will free one from the useless agitation of the material senses, which drive one to wander throughout the world searching in vain for material happiness. Lord Śrī Caitanya Mahāprabhu has also emphasized the tree’s quality of tolerance: taror iva sahiṣṇunā, kīrtanīyaḥ sadā hariḥ. One who is as tolerant as a tree can chant the holy name of Kṛṣṇa constantly, finding ever-new satisfaction.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    A saintly person should learn from the mountain to devote all his efforts to the service of others and to make the welfare of others the sole reason for his existence. Similarly, as the disciple of the tree, he should learn to dedicate himself to others. He speaks of the mountain and the tree, which also represent the earth. The mountain always devotes its efforts for others by holding up the earth, producing waterfalls and giving jewels. The devotee should learn this conduct from the mountain. As the disciple of the tree, he should learn to dedicate himself completely to others. One can take the tree from one place to another, plant it and water it. The tree accepts this, and does not protest. The yogī should be like that. This is the particular nature of the tree not seen in the mountain.
    Personal Guidance
    Learn from the mountain and the tree: exist for others, give without protest, and let tolerance become the soil in which constant remembrance of Kṛṣṇa grows.
    Practical Applications
    • Pick one resource you guard — time, money, skill — and spend a measurable portion of it today serving someone who cannot repay you.
    • When someone cuts into you with criticism or demand, practice taror iva sahiṣṇunā: do not protest, and continue offering what service you can.
    • Before sleep, dedicate today's earnings and efforts explicitly to the pleasure of the spiritual master and Kṛṣṇa, refusing the thought that they were 'yours' to begin with.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where in my life am I still demanding that my service be recognized, and how would a mountain or tree act in that same situation?
    • What 'cutting down' am I currently resisting — and what would it mean to keep serving from that very wound?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • In your friend group or hostel, identify the person everyone overlooks and quietly do one concrete service for them today without telling anyone.
    • When a classmate takes credit for your work or a teacher is unfair, practice not protesting outwardly — write the reaction in your journal instead and offer the sting to Kṛṣṇa.
    • Refuse the social-media logic that says service only counts if it is seen; do one good act this week that you tell no one about, not even online.
    householder
    • Review this month's spending and reassign a clear percentage to the service of devotees, the spiritual master's mission, or a person in genuine need — make parārtha a line item, not a leftover.
    • When your spouse, child, or aged parent 'cuts into' your evening with an inconvenient demand, treat it as the tree being chopped and respond with service rather than negotiation or sigh.
    • In a work conflict this week, choose the response that protects the other person's dignity even at cost to your own position, and dedicate that cost to Kṛṣṇa before bed.
    senior
    • Identify the knowledge, contacts, or possessions you have been quietly hoarding 'for later' and begin transferring them now to younger devotees and family members who can use them in Kṛṣṇa's service.
    • When the body's decline 'cuts you down' — pain, dependency, being passed over — practice taror iva sahiṣṇunā and use that very tolerance as the ground for steadier chanting of the holy name.
    • Become a mountain for your grandchildren and juniors: let them draw freely from your time, stories, and patience, expecting nothing in return, and aim every such gift at their eventual remembrance of Kṛṣṇa.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Mistaking doormat passivity for tree-like tolerance, so that one absorbs abuse without any inner offering to Kṛṣṇa.
    • Performing visible philanthropy while keeping the best of one's wealth and energy for one's own sense gratification.
    • Reducing the verse to material humanitarianism — feeding bodies while ignoring the soul's need for Kṛṣṇa consciousness, which is the real parārtha.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Share a recent moment when you were 'cut down' — did you protest, withdraw, or keep serving? What does the tree's example expose in your response?
    • Is there a difference between selflessness taught by modern ethics and the parārthaikānta-sambhavaḥ of this verse? Where do they part ways?
    • Whose welfare do you currently treat as the 'sole reason' for your existence? Be honest — name the person or thing, and weigh it against what this verse asks.
    Role Play

    A householder student has worked overtime for weeks on a project; a colleague takes public credit and the manager scolds the student for a minor error. That evening the student's spouse asks for help with the children and an elderly neighbor knocks asking for a ride to the hospital. Two students enact the scene — one playing the householder, one playing spouse/colleague/neighbor in turn — and the group then discusses what mountain-like and tree-like responses would actually look like, moment by moment, without collapsing into either resentment or fake saintliness.

    Objections & Responses
    • If I live only for others, I will be exploited and burn out — this is unhealthy, not spiritual.
      The verse does not ask you to serve your own false ego's image of being useful; it asks you to make parārtha — the welfare of others, ultimately their relationship with Kṛṣṇa — the axis of your life. A mountain is not depleted by giving water, because it is fed by clouds from above; a sādhu is sustained by Kṛṣṇa, not by the gratitude of those served. Burnout comes from serving for one's own subtle return, not from genuine parārthaikānta-sambhavaḥ.
    • Trees and mountains are insentient — comparing a conscious human being to them romanticizes inertia and passivity.
      Prabhupāda's purport is precise: we are to learn specific qualities — tolerance, magnanimity, sustenance of many — not to imitate insentience. Lord Caitanya himself cited taror iva sahiṣṇunā as the qualification for constant kīrtana, which is the most active, conscious engagement possible. Tree-like tolerance is the inner posture that frees the senses from agitation, so that real service and chanting become possible.

    A learned sage should take his satisfaction in the simple maintenance of his existence and should not seek satisfaction through gratifying the material senses. In other words, one should care for the material body in such a way that one’s higher knowledge is not destroyed and so that one’s speech and mind are not deviated from self-realization.
    Purport

    A wise man does not absorb his consciousness in the forms, flavors, aromas and sensations of material sense gratification, but rather accepts activities such as eating and sleeping simply to keep body and soul together. One must properly maintain one’s body by regulated activities of eating, sleeping, cleansing, etc., otherwise the mind will become weak, and one’s spiritual knowledge will fade away. If one eats too austerely, or if in the name of selflessness one accepts impure food, surely one loses control of the mind. On the other hand, if one eats food that is excessively fatty or rich there will be an unwanted increase in sleep and semen, and thus the mind and speech will be overwhelmed by the modes of passion and ignorance. Lord Kṛṣṇa has summarized the whole matter in Bhagavad-gītā by His statement yuktāhāra-vihārasya yukta-ceṣṭasya karmasu. One should moderately and intelligently regulate all of one’s bodily activities so that they are favorable for self-realization. This technique is taught by the bona fide spiritual master. If one is too austere or if one engages too much in sense gratification, self-realization is impossible.

    It is the duty of a devotee of the Lord to avoid seeing any object as separate from Kṛṣṇa, because that is illusion. A gentleman will never try to enjoy the property of another gentleman. Similarly, if one sees everything in relation to Kṛṣṇa, there is no scope for material sense gratification. But if one sees material objects as separate from Kṛṣṇa, then one’s material enjoying propensity is immediately aroused. A human being must be intelligent enough to distinguish between preyas, or temporary gratification, and śreyas, permanent benefit. One may accept sense activity in a regulated, limited fashion so that one will be strong for serving Kṛṣṇa, but if one excessively indulges the material senses, one will lose one’s gravity and seriousness in spiritual life and act like an ordinary materialist. The ultimate goal, as stated here, is jṣānam, or steady consciousness of the Absolute Truth, Lord Kṛṣṇa.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    A learned sage should take his satisfaction with the actions of his prāṇa and should not seek satisfaction through the sense objects. In other words, one should care for the material body in such a way that one’s higher knowledge is not destroyed and so that one’s speech and mind are not deviated from self-realization. There are two types of air: prāṇa and the external air. This verse speaks of what he learned from prāṇa. Prāṇa operates by eating and other actions, and is not dependent on the objects of the senses like form and taste (indriya-priyaih). By taking satisfaction from the prāṇa he becomes a sage. Jṣāna will be destroyed by disturbance of the mind, caused by disruption of the prāṇa. Therefore one should maintain the body by eating etc., but in such a way that speech and mind will not create disturbance. The mind will become disturbed by eating course or impure food. The mind and speech will be agitated by food which is too oily, because of increase in laziness and semen.
    Related lectures
    • Balaram Shakti Pr SB 11-07-39-44 - GEV
      His Grace Balaram Shakti Prabhu· English
    Personal Guidance
    Eat, sleep, and care for the body only enough to keep jṣāna intact — never let the senses dictate the terms of your sādhana.
    Practical Applications
    • Set today's meals at the threshold of bodily sufficiency — enough to serve Kṛṣṇa clearly, not enough to thicken sleep or stir rajas.
    • Notice one indulgence you justify as 'maintenance' (a richer dish, an extra hour of sleep, a stimulating feed) and cut it back today.
    • Before any sense engagement, ask whether you are seeing the object as separate from Kṛṣṇa or in relation to Him, and refuse the first.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where am I dressing up indriya-priya as prāṇa-vṛtti — calling sense pleasure mere upkeep — and what knowledge has quietly faded as a result?
    • In the last week, when did my speech or mind get scattered (nāvakīryeta vāṅ-manaḥ), and which 'innocent' bodily indulgence preceded it?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • Audit your phone and feed today: cut one stream that is pure indriya-priya (short-form video, gossip threads) and notice how speech and study steady within hours.
    • Eat your hostel or campus meals on a schedule that keeps you alert for class and japa, not heavy and sleepy — refuse the late-night junk run even when friends insist.
    • Before chasing the next 'experience' your peers are pushing (party, binge, hookup, all-nighter), ask whether it will protect or erode your capacity to study śāstra this week.
    householder
    • Set the family's table by yuktāhāra — moderate portions, sāttvika food, fixed times — so that children grow up tasting prāṇa-vṛtti rather than indriya-priya as the norm.
    • Review one 'lifestyle upgrade' the family is considering (richer food, bigger home, more entertainment) against the test: will it strengthen or fade our collective remembrance of Kṛṣṇa?
    • Schedule sleep, work, and recreation around morning sādhana and evening hearing, not the other way around — let earning and enjoying serve self-realization, not displace it.
    senior
    • Simplify your diet and daily comforts now, deliberately — lighter food, earlier sleep, fewer stimulations — so the mind is clear for hearing, chanting, and remembrance in the years that remain.
    • Mentor a younger devotee specifically on yuktāhāra-vihāra: show, from your own long experience, how over-austerity and over-indulgence both wrecked sādhana, and how regulation protected jṣāna.
    • Loosen one long-held bodily attachment (a favorite rich food, a habitual comfort, a treasured possession) as a concrete rehearsal for the final letting-go, keeping speech and mind fixed on Kṛṣṇa.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Swinging into harsh austerity, eating impure or insufficient food in the name of renunciation, and then losing mental control entirely.
    • Swinging the other way — calling rich, heavy, over-stimulating intake 'prasāda' or 'taking care of the body' while sleep and passion swell.
    • Treating yuktāhāra-vihāra as a private formula one can self-calibrate, bypassing the guidance of a bona fide spiritual master.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Compare your last three meals: which were truly prāṇa-vṛtti and which were indriya-priya dressed up as maintenance — and how do you tell the difference in your own life?
    • Where is the line between caring properly for the body so jṣāna is not destroyed and pampering the body so jṣāna fades — and who in your life draws that line for you?
    • Share a concrete moment when over-austerity or over-indulgence visibly disturbed your speech or mind, and what you learned about preyas vs. śreyas from it.
    Role Play

    A new devotee invites a senior student to dinner and serves an elaborate, very rich, very sweet 'offered' feast, insisting that since it is prasāda there can be no excess. The senior student must accept the hospitality with grace, honor the offering, and yet hold the line of yuktāhāra — without shaming the host or pretending the verse does not apply. Two students play the host and guest; a third observes and reports where indriya-priya was disguised as devotion.

    Objections & Responses
    • This sounds like life-denying asceticism dressed in Sanskrit — modern wellness teaches that listening to the body's appetites is health, not bondage.
      The verse explicitly rejects both extremes: too austere and the mind collapses, too indulgent and rajas and tamas overwhelm speech and mind. Kṛṣṇa's own word in the Gītā is yuktāhāra-vihārasya — regulated, not denied. The standard is not suppression of the body but protection of jṣāna; the body is kept fit precisely so that higher knowledge does not fade.
    • If everything can be seen in relation to Kṛṣṇa, then I can enjoy whatever I want and simply 'offer' it — the verse should not restrict me.
      Seeing things in relation to Kṛṣṇa is the opposite of using His name to license enjoyment. The verse warns that the moment you treat the object as separate from Him — as yours to enjoy — material propensity is aroused. The test is honest: after the 'offered' indulgence, are speech and mind steadier in Kṛṣṇa, or scattered? The answer, not the label, decides whether it was prāṇa-vṛtti or indriya-priya.

    • Set the family's table by yuktāhāra — moderate portions, sāttvika food, fixed times — so that children grow up tasting prāṇa-vṛtti rather than indriya-priya as the norm.
    • Review one 'lifestyle upgrade' the family is considering (richer food, bigger home, more entertainment) against the test: will it strengthen or fade our collective remembrance of Kṛṣṇa?
    • Schedule sleep, work, and recreation around morning sādhana and evening hearing, not the other way around — let earning and enjoying serve self-realization, not displace it.
    senior
    • Simplify your diet and daily comforts now, deliberately — lighter food, earlier sleep, fewer stimulations — so the mind is clear for hearing, chanting, and remembrance in the years that remain.
    • Mentor a younger devotee specifically on yuktāhāra-vihāra: show, from your own long experience, how over-austerity and over-indulgence both wrecked sādhana, and how regulation protected jṣāna.
    • Loosen one long-held bodily attachment (a favorite rich food, a habitual comfort, a treasured possession) as a concrete rehearsal for the final letting-go, keeping speech and mind fixed on Kṛṣṇa.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Swinging into harsh austerity, eating impure or insufficient food in the name of renunciation, and then losing mental control entirely.
    • Swinging the other way — calling rich, heavy, over-stimulating intake 'prasāda' or 'taking care of the body' while sleep and passion swell.
    • Treating yuktāhāra-vihāra as a private formula one can self-calibrate, bypassing the guidance of a bona fide spiritual master.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Compare your last three meals: which were truly prāṇa-vṛtti and which were indriya-priya dressed up as maintenance — and how do you tell the difference in your own life?
    • Where is the line between caring properly for the body so jṣāna is not destroyed and pampering the body so jṣāna fades — and who in your life draws that line for you?
    • Share a concrete moment when over-austerity or over-indulgence visibly disturbed your speech or mind, and what you learned about preyas vs. śreyas from it.
    Role Play

    A new devotee invites a senior student to dinner and serves an elaborate, very rich, very sweet 'offered' feast, insisting that since it is prasāda there can be no excess. The senior student must accept the hospitality with grace, honor the offering, and yet hold the line of yuktāhāra — without shaming the host or pretending the verse does not apply. Two students play the host and guest; a third observes and reports where indriya-priya was disguised as devotion.

    Objections & Responses
    • This sounds like life-denying asceticism dressed in Sanskrit — modern wellness teaches that listening to the body's appetites is health, not bondage.
      The verse explicitly rejects both extremes: too austere and the mind collapses, too indulgent and rajas and tamas overwhelm speech and mind. Kṛṣṇa's own word in the Gītā is yuktāhāra-vihārasya — regulated, not denied. The standard is not suppression of the body but protection of jṣāna; the body is kept fit precisely so that higher knowledge does not fade.
    • If everything can be seen in relation to Kṛṣṇa, then I can enjoy whatever I want and simply 'offer' it — the verse should not restrict me.
      Seeing things in relation to Kṛṣṇa is the opposite of using His name to license enjoyment. The verse warns that the moment you treat the object as separate from Him — as yours to enjoy — material propensity is aroused. The test is honest: after the 'offered' indulgence, are speech and mind steadier in Kṛṣṇa, or scattered? The answer, not the label, decides whether it was prāṇa-vṛtti or indriya-priya.
    📝 My note

    Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam 11.7.40

    ↗
    విషయేష్వావిశన్ యోగీ నానాధర్మేషు సర్వత: । గుణదోషవ్యపేతాత్మా న విషజ్జేత వాయువత్ ॥ ౪౦ ॥
    viṣayeṣv āviśan yogī
    [vishayeshv aavishan yogee]
    nānā-dharmeṣu sarvataḥ
    [naanaa-dharmeshu sarvatah]

    [guna-dosha-vyapetaatmaa]
    na viṣajjeta vāyu-vat
    [na vishajjeta vaayu-vat]
    Word-for-word
    viṣayeṣu — into contact with material objects āviśan — entering yogī — one who has attained self-control nānā-dharmeṣu — which have different varieties of qualities sarvataḥ — everywhere guṇa — good qualities doṣa — and faults vyapeta-ātmā — a person who has transcended na viṣajjeta — should not become entangled vāyu-vat — like the wind.
    Blended reading (Sanskrit + English inline)

    āviśan

    yogī

    nānā-dharmeṣu sarvataḥ
    nānā-dharmeṣu

    sarvataḥ

    like the wind.
    Even a transcendentalist is surrounded by innumerable material objects, which possess good and bad qualities. However, one who has transcended material good and evil should not become entangled even when in contact with the material objects; rather, he should act like the wind.
    Purport

    The wind is the external manifestation of air, whereas prāṇa is the internal manifestation. When the wind passes over waterfalls it carries sprinkles of clear water and thus becomes most refreshing. Sometimes the wind blows through a beautiful forest, carrying the fragrances of fruits and flowers; at other times the wind may fuel a fire that burns the same forest to ashes. The wind, however, being fixed in its own nature, remains neutral in both its auspicious and inauspicious activities. Similarly, within this material world we will inevitably face both pleasing and disgusting situations. If, however, we remain fixed in Kṛṣṇa consciousness, we will not be disturbed by the inauspicious, nor will we become attached to the materially auspicious. In the course of his spiritual duties, a devotee sometimes finds himself chanting Hare Kṛṣṇa in a beautiful country atmosphere, and sometimes he finds himself doing the same thing in a hellish city. In both cases the devotee fixes his mind upon Lord Kṛṣṇa and experiences transcendental bliss. Although the wind passes through the most dark and forbidding places, the wind is not frightened or disturbed. Similarly, a devotee of Lord Kṛṣṇa should never be fearful or anxious, even when in the most difficult situation. One who is attached to materially pleasing forms, tastes, smells, sounds and touches will also be repelled by the opposite in each category. Thus finding himself surrounded by innumerable good and bad things, the materialist is constantly disturbed. When the wind blows in many directions at once, the atmosphere becomes agitated. Similarly, if the mind is constantly attracted and repelled by material objects there will be such mental disturbance that it will be impossible to think of the Absolute Truth. Therefore, one should learn from the blowing wind the art of moving throughout the material world without attachment.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    The yogī, indifferent to good and bad qualities, though contacting sense objects of various qualities, is not attached to them, just like the air. Though one indulges in sense objects, one remains unattached to them. One learns this from the external air. The yogī contacts objects which are light or heavy, excellent or inferior, but is not attached to any of them. The air is not attached to either a dark cave or a blazing fire.
    Personal Guidance
    Move through the material world like the wind — touching pleasant and unpleasant alike, fixed in Kṛṣṇa, neither attached nor repelled.
    Practical Applications
    • Notice the first object today that pulls you toward attraction or aversion, and consciously pass through it like wind — registering it without clinging.
    • Chant your rounds with the same attention in a noisy commute as in a quiet room, refusing to make your sādhana depend on pleasant surroundings.
    • Refuse to rearrange your day around chasing one viṣaya or escaping another — keep your duty and remembrance of Kṛṣṇa fixed regardless of the setting.
    Reflection Questions
    • Which pleasant sense object am I quietly arranging my life around, and what unpleasant one am I equally arranging my life to avoid?
    • Where do I mistake the wind's neutrality for indifference, and how is real vairāgya different from cold detachment in my own conduct?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • When the group chat erupts in drama or a post goes viral against you, practice passing through it like wind — read, register, return to your study or japa without being pulled in.
    • Walk into your next exam or interview without rehearsing either the dream outcome or the disaster — show up, do the work, let the result blow past you.
    • Notice how friend groups try to fix you as 'the fun one' or 'the serious one'; refuse to be defined by their praise or teasing, and keep your own sādhana steady.
    householder
    • When your spouse, child, or boss brings a wave of praise or blame home today, receive it fully but do not let the household's mood for the evening be set by it.
    • Make one financial or career decision this week based on duty and Kṛṣṇa's service rather than on chasing a pleasant outcome or fleeing an unpleasant one.
    • In raising your children, hold the same tone whether they have just made you proud or just embarrassed you — let them see a parent fixed in something deeper than their performance.
    senior
    • As the body brings new discomforts and the world brings new losses, practice letting each pass through you like wind through a forest, without making it the center of your inner life.
    • Loosen your grip on one comfort — a chair, a routine, a possession — that you have been quietly arranging your day around, and see what remains when it is gone.
    • When mentoring younger devotees or family, speak from wind-like steadiness rather than from nostalgia for pleasant pasts or fear of an unpleasant future.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Mistaking dullness, suppression, or emotional shutdown for the wind-like neutrality the verse describes.
    • Using 'I am like the wind' as a rationalization to enter risky sense-environments, when the verse presupposes one already transcends guṇa-doṣa.
    • Becoming proud of equipoise in pleasant settings while still being inwardly disturbed when conditions turn hellish.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Share one situation this week where you were clearly attached to a guṇa or repelled by a doṣa — what would acting like the wind have looked like concretely?
    • Does 'act like the wind' mean we should stop having preferences about our environment, or something subtler? Where do you and your partner disagree?
    • Prabhupāda says the devotee chants the same in a beautiful country and a hellish city — is that realistic for us now, or an ideal we are far from? Be honest with each other.
    Role Play

    One student is a devotee who has just been reassigned from a peaceful rural āśrama to serve in a loud, polluted, morally chaotic city neighborhood; the other is a sympathetic friend urging them to refuse the move 'for their spiritual health.' Play the conversation using this verse — the devotee must explain wind-like steadiness without sounding cold or self-righteous.

    Objections & Responses
    • Acting like the wind sounds like emotional repression — psychologically this seems unhealthy and even dangerous.
      The verse is not asking us to suppress feeling but to stop being tossed by every attraction and aversion. The wind is not numb; it moves freely, carries fragrance, even fans fire — yet it is not owned by any of these. A devotee fixed in Kṛṣṇa still feels, still serves, still weeps in kīrtana, but is no longer captured by guṇa and doṣa. That is freedom, not repression.
    • If I should be unaffected by good and bad alike, why bother choosing a sāttvic environment, good association, or wholesome work at all?
      Notice the verse says guṇa-doṣa-vyapetātmā — one whose self has already transcended material good and evil. Until that stage, we very much need favorable conditions, sādhu-saṅga, and regulated life; that is the ladder. The wind-like stage is the fruit of disciplined sādhana, not a license to skip it. We choose sattva precisely so that one day no environment can disturb our remembrance of Kṛṣṇa.

    Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam 11.7.41

    ↗
    పార్థివేష్విహ దేహేషు ప్రవిష్టస్తద్గుణాశ్రయ: । గుణైర్న యుజ్యతే యోగీ గన్ధైర్వాయురివాత్మద‍ృక్ ॥ ౪౧ ॥
    pārthiveṣv iha deheṣu
    [paarthiveshv iha deheshu]
    praviṣṭas tad-guṇāśrayaḥ

    Although a self-realized soul may live in various material bodies while in this world, experiencing their various qualities and functions, he is never entangled, just as the wind which carries various aromas does not actually mix with them.
    Purport

    Although we experience the wind as fragrant or foul, depending on the aromas it carries, the wind does not in fact change its actual nature. Similarly, although we regard a particular person as strong or weak, intelligent or retarded, beautiful or homely, good or bad, the pure spirit soul, who is the actual person, does not really possess any of the qualities of the body but is merely covered by them, just as the wind is covered by different aromas. Thus, a Kṛṣṇa conscious person is always aware that he is different from the temporary body. He experiences the various transformations of the body, such as childhood, adolescence, adulthood and old age; but although he experiences the pains, pleasures, qualities and functions of that body, a Kṛṣṇa conscious person never thinks that he is the body. He always understands that he is an eternal spirit soul, part and parcel of Lord Kṛṣṇa. As stated in this verse, na yujyate yogī: he is not entangled. The conclusion is that one should never consider a Kṛṣṇa conscious person in terms of bodily designation, but should see him as an eternal servitor of the Lord.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Although a self-realized soul may live in various material bodies while in this world, experiencing their various qualities and functions, he is never entangled by those qualities, just as the wind which carries various aromas does not actually mix with them. One should learn from the air that one should remain unattached to the qualities of the body. The air does not mix with good or bad fragrance though it is aware of them by contacting them. Though the yogī is aware of his contact with the qualities of the body he is not those qualities because he sees that the ātmā is different from them.
    Related lectures
    • MG SB 11-07-41-45 - Krishna inst Uddhava - 2007-01-06 Rajkot
      His Holiness Mahavishnu Goswami· 2007-01-06· English
    • RGS SB 11-07-41-44 Hindi - Twenty-Four Guru-13
      His Holiness Radha Govinda Swami· English
    Personal Guidance
    Like wind that carries scents without becoming them, the self-realized yogī moves through bodies and their qualities untouched, knowing he is not the body.
    Practical Applications
    • Notice today when you accept a bodily label — "I am tired," "I am clever," "I am ugly" — and silently correct it to "this body is, but I am the soul covered by it."
    • When someone praises or insults your appearance, intelligence, or status, receive it as wind passing through and refuse to let it settle as your self-definition.
    • Spend ten minutes recalling your own childhood, adolescence, and present body, and feel the single witness who has carried all of them without becoming any.
    Reflection Questions
    • Which quality of my current body — its strength, weakness, beauty, or dullness — have I most quietly mistaken for my actual self, and what does that confusion cost my bhakti?
    • If the wind is not stained by the aromas it carries, what would it look like for me to walk through today's pleasures and pains as a yogī rather than as their owner?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • When your social media feed rewards or shames you for your face, body, or cleverness, name silently: "this is an aroma the wind is carrying today, not me."
    • Before an exam or audition, remind yourself that the result will label your body and résumé — not your soul — and then prepare and act with full effort anyway.
    • In a friend group that ranks people by looks, intelligence, or popularity, refuse to rank yourself or others by those bodily qualities even once today.
    householder
    • When your spouse or children criticize a quality of your body or temperament, receive it as feedback for the covering, not as a verdict on the soul, and respond without defensiveness.
    • In career setbacks or promotions, notice whether you are identifying with the title and salary attached to this body, and re-anchor in your identity as Kṛṣṇa's servant before reacting.
    • Raise your children to distinguish their bodily designations (smart, athletic, shy) from their selves by speaking to the soul in them, not only to their performance.
    senior
    • As the body weakens, practice watching each new limitation arrive like a fresh aroma on the wind — acknowledge it, serve through it, but do not let it become your name.
    • When mentoring younger devotees or family members, model this verse by refusing to introduce yourself through past achievements of the body and résumé.
    • Prepare for death by daily rehearsing the truth that the soul who passed through your childhood and adulthood will pass through this final transition equally uncovered.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Using "I am not this body" as an excuse to neglect the body's duties, health, or service capacity rather than as a meditation that frees one for service.
    • Sliding into impersonalist detachment — treating the soul as a generic witness — instead of remembering the soul is Kṛṣṇa's eternal servitor passing through bodies.
    • Judging others by their bodily designations (caste, looks, intellect, age) while claiming to know that the soul within is distinct from the covering.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Share one bodily quality you privately identify with — and discuss whether seeing yourself as the wind rather than the aroma would loosen or tighten your grip on it.
    • The verse says the yogī experiences the guṇas without mixing with them. In your own life, where is the line between healthy experience and entangled identification?
    • If a Kṛṣṇa conscious person should never be judged by bodily designation, how do we still honor varṇāśrama duties without collapsing the soul into the body?
    Role Play

    One student plays a practitioner who has just been told by a doctor that a chronic illness will progress; another plays a godbrother who must speak from this verse — not minimizing the body's pain, not spiritualizing it away, but helping the first see himself as the wind passing through this particular aroma.

    Objections & Responses
    • This sounds like dissociation — telling people their suffering or their gifts aren't really theirs seems psychologically unhealthy and even dangerous.
      The verse does not deny that the body experiences pain and pleasure; it denies that those experiences define the soul. A yogī feels the body's transformations fully — childhood, old age, sickness — but does not collapse his identity into them, which is the opposite of dissociation: it is the steadiness that lets him serve through every condition.
    • If the soul is unaffected by the body's qualities, why bother with sādhana, varṇāśrama, or even caring for the body at all?
      Precisely because the soul is covered by these bodily aromas, sādhana is needed to remember its true nature and serve Kṛṣṇa through whatever body is given. The verse describes the mature yogī's vision, not a license for negligence; the body remains the field where bhakti is practiced and offered.

    • Judging others by their bodily designations (caste, looks, intellect, age) while claiming to know that the soul within is distinct from the covering.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Share one bodily quality you privately identify with — and discuss whether seeing yourself as the wind rather than the aroma would loosen or tighten your grip on it.
    • The verse says the yogī experiences the guṇas without mixing with them. In your own life, where is the line between healthy experience and entangled identification?
    • If a Kṛṣṇa conscious person should never be judged by bodily designation, how do we still honor varṇāśrama duties without collapsing the soul into the body?
    Role Play

    One student plays a practitioner who has just been told by a doctor that a chronic illness will progress; another plays a godbrother who must speak from this verse — not minimizing the body's pain, not spiritualizing it away, but helping the first see himself as the wind passing through this particular aroma.

    Objections & Responses
    • This sounds like dissociation — telling people their suffering or their gifts aren't really theirs seems psychologically unhealthy and even dangerous.
      The verse does not deny that the body experiences pain and pleasure; it denies that those experiences define the soul. A yogī feels the body's transformations fully — childhood, old age, sickness — but does not collapse his identity into them, which is the opposite of dissociation: it is the steadiness that lets him serve through every condition.
    • If the soul is unaffected by the body's qualities, why bother with sādhana, varṇāśrama, or even caring for the body at all?
      Precisely because the soul is covered by these bodily aromas, sādhana is needed to remember its true nature and serve Kṛṣṇa through whatever body is given. The verse describes the mature yogī's vision, not a license for negligence; the body remains the field where bhakti is practiced and offered.

    A thoughtful sage, even while living within a material body, should understand himself to be pure spirit soul. Similarly, one should see that the spirit soul enters within all forms of life, both moving and nonmoving, and that the individual souls are thus all-pervading. The sage should further observe that the Supreme Personality of Godhead, as the Supersoul, is simultaneously present within all things. Both the individual soul and the Supersoul can be understood by comparing them to the nature of the sky: although the sky extends everywhere and everything rests within the sky, the sky does not mix with anything, nor can it be divided by anything.
    Purport

    Although air exists within the sky, the sky, or space, is different from air. Even in the absence of air, space or sky is present. All material objects are situated within space, or within the vast material sky, but the sky remains undivided and, although accommodating all objects, never actually mixes with anything. In the same way one can understand the situation of both the individual soul and the Supersoul. The individual soul is all-pervading, because there are innumerable jīvātmās, which enter within all things; yet, as confirmed in Vedic literature, each individual ātmā remains infinitesimal. The Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad (5.9) states:

    bālāgra-śata-bhāgasya śatadhā kalpitasya ca bhāgo jīvaḥ sa vijṣeyaḥ sa cānantyāya kalpate

    “When the upper point of a hair is divided into one hundred parts and again each of such parts is further divided into one hundred parts, each such part is the measurement of the dimension of the spirit soul.” The same is stated in Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam:

    keśāgra-śata-bhāgasya śatāṁśaḥ sādṛśātmakaḥ jīvaḥ sūkṣma-svarūpo ’yaṁ saṅkhyātīto hi cit-kaṇaḥ

    “There are innumerable particles of spiritual atoms, which are measured as one ten-thousandth of the upper portion of the hair.”

    The Supreme Personality of Godhead, however, is all-pervading because He Himself is personally present everywhere. The Lord is known as advaita, or indivisible. Thus the same unique Personality of Godhead exists everywhere, just like the sky, and yet is not attached to anything, although everything is resting within Him. The Lord Himself has confirmed this analysis of His all-pervasiveness in Bhagavad-gītā (9.6) :

    yathākāśa-sthito nityaṁ vāyuḥ sarvatra-go mahān tathā sarvāṇi bhūtāni mat-sthānīty upadhāraya

    “As the almighty wind, blowing everywhere, always rests in ethereal space, know that in the same manner all beings rest in Me.”

    Therefore, although both the jīva soul and the Supersoul are said to be all-pervading, it should be remembered that there are innumerable individual jīva souls, whereas there is only one Supreme Personality of Godhead. The Lord is always supreme, and one who is actually a thoughtful sage never doubts the supreme position of the Lord.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    The yogī should meditate on Paramātmā, spreading everywhere and undivided as the medium called Brahman in all moving and non-moving beings, inside and outside, similar to ether. Seeing the ether, one learns that though Paramātmā is inside and outside everything, he is not attached to anything. This is explained in two verses. The yogī should meditate with intelligence on Paramātmā who is like ether, pervading everywhere inside and outside. Paramātmā is undivided, spreading everything as a connecting medium in the form of Brahman in all moving and non-moving beings, just as ether though pervading everywhere, does not mix with the pot or other objects and does not become divided.
    Related lectures
    • Akuti Mataji SB 11-07-42 - 2017-04-12 ISKCON Alachua
      Her Grace Akuti Mataji· 2017-04-12· English
    Personal Guidance
    Like the sky that holds everything yet mixes with nothing, the soul and the Supersoul pervade all bodies while remaining untouched — live as that unmixed witness today.
    Practical Applications
    • Each time your body reports a sensation today — hunger, fatigue, pleasure — silently note: "this is happening in me, not to me," and return to the witnessing ātmā.
    • When you meet a person, animal, or even a plant today, pause for one breath and acknowledge the same jīva-ātmā within them, accompanied by Kṛṣṇa as Supersoul.
    • Refuse to let one stinging word or one flattering word "stick" — recall the sky-nature of the soul and let the remark pass through without coloring you.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where in my day do I most forget the sky-nature of the soul and start identifying as the air, the dust, and the weather passing through it?
    • If Kṛṣṇa as Supersoul is already present within every being I will meet today, what in my behavior toward them would I have to change to honor that fact?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • Next time a comment on your post or a grade on an exam tries to define you, name it out loud as "weather in the sky" of the ātmā and refuse to let it set your mood for the day.
    • In your friend group today, pick the person you find most irritating and silently acknowledge Kṛṣṇa as Supersoul seated within them before you speak a single word.
    • When peer pressure pushes you to perform an identity — cool, smart, edgy — pause and ask which "air" you are mistaking for the sky of your real self.
    householder
    • In one charged interaction with spouse or child today, consciously hold the sky-vision: their behavior is passing weather, the ātmā within them — and Kṛṣṇa within that — is whom you are actually serving.
    • Before a money or career decision this week, sit for two minutes and locate yourself as the unmixed witness, so the decision is made by the sage in you, not by the anxieties moving through you.
    • When raising your children, speak to the jīva in them at least once a day — a word of respect, a serious question — alongside all the practical instruction you must give the body and mind.
    senior
    • As the body's capacities visibly contract, deliberately rehearse the sky-nature of the ātmā each morning, so that aging becomes confirmation of the verse rather than a private grief.
    • Identify one attachment — a possession, a role, a grievance — and consciously let it pass through you this month the way wind passes through sky, offering the release to Kṛṣṇa as Supersoul.
    • When mentoring younger people, address the soul within them, not merely their career or behavior; let them feel that someone finally saw the sky in them, not just the weather.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Sliding from "the soul is like the sky" into impersonalism — treating the Supersoul as mere space or consciousness rather than Kṛṣṇa personally present within all.
    • Using "I am untouched spirit soul" as a spiritual alibi for neglecting bodily duties, family, and sevā, when the verse asks for vision, not negligence.
    • Collapsing the distinction between the innumerable infinitesimal jīvas and the one all-pervading Supreme — flattening "all is one" instead of seeing one Lord within many souls.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Share a recent moment when an insult or a compliment clearly "stuck" to you — what would it have looked like, concretely, to remain sky-like in that moment, and was that even desirable?
    • The verse insists the soul is all-pervading yet infinitesimal, and the Supersoul is all-pervading yet one — where do you find yourself blurring these two, and why does the distinction matter for bhakti?
    • If every moving and non-moving being already has Kṛṣṇa within as Supersoul, how should that change the way we treat the people we find most difficult — and where do you resist that conclusion?
    Role Play

    Two students are paired. Student A has just been passed over for a promotion at work and vents bitterly about a colleague who got it; Student B, drawing on this verse, must respond — not by dismissing the pain, but by gently helping A see the sky-nature of the ātmā, the Supersoul present even in the colleague, without sliding into platitudes like "let it go" or impersonalist talk of "we are all one."

    Objections & Responses
    • If the soul is truly untouched like the sky, then nothing I do to my body or to others really matters — this teaching seems to license indifference.
      The verse describes the soul's ontological nature, not a permission slip for the conditioned self. Precisely because Kṛṣṇa as Supersoul dwells in every being, every action toward every body becomes a transaction with Him; the sky-nature is realized by the sage who serves more carefully, not less.
    • "All-pervading individual souls" and "one all-pervading Supreme" sounds like contradictory metaphysics smuggled in to protect a personal God.
      Gauḍīya ācāryas read this as acintya-bheda-abheda: the jīvas are innumerable and atomic in size yet collectively pervade through their presence in all bodies, while Kṛṣṇa is one and personally all-pervading as Supersoul. The sky analogy is meant to hold both truths together, not to dissolve one into the other.

    Although the mighty wind blows clouds and storms across the sky, the sky is never implicated or affected by these activities. Similarly, the spirit soul is not actually changed or affected by contact with the material nature. Although the living entity enters within a body made of earth, water and fire, and although he is impelled by the three modes of nature created by eternal time, his eternal spiritual nature is never actually affected.
    Purport

    Although the sky appears to be affected by the mighty movements of wind, rain, hurricanes, lightning and thunder, etc., the sky, being very subtle, is actually not affected, but is rather the background for such visible activities. Similarly, although the material body and mind undergo innumerable changes, such as birth and death, happiness and distress, love and hate, the eternal living entity is merely the background for such activities. The spirit soul, being most subtle, is not actually affected; only due to misidentification with the superficial activities of the body and mind does the soul undergo terrible distress within the material world.

    In this regard, Śrīla Madhvācārya has pointed out that the individual living entity must struggle to revive his divine spiritual qualities. The living entity is part and parcel of the supreme entity, called Kṛṣṇa, and as such the individual soul is also a reservoir of godly qualities. The Personality of Godhead, however, automatically manifests these qualities without any hindrance, whereas the conditioned soul must struggle to revive such qualities. Thus, although both the Personality of Godhead and the personality of the living entity are eternal and transcendental, the Personality of Godhead is always supreme. By realizing all this with clear intelligence, the conditioned soul can rise to the spiritual platform.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Just as ether is not touched by clouds blown by the wind, the jīva is not touched by the body made of fire, water, and earth by time. The jīva is not touched by the body etc. (guṇaiḥ) which is created by time, composed of fire, water and earth, just as ether is not touched by clouds blown by the wind.
    Personal Guidance
    Like the sky untouched by storms it holds, the soul is never truly altered by the body's turbulence — only misidentification makes the wind feel like a wound.
    Practical Applications
    • Notice one strong emotional weather-front today — anger, anxiety, elation — and silently name yourself the sky, not the cloud passing through.
    • When the body signals pain, hunger, or fatigue, pause and say plainly: this belongs to earth, water, and fire — I am the witness behind it.
    • End the day by reviewing one event where you over-identified with a guṇa-driven reaction, and offer that misidentification to Kṛṣṇa before sleep.
    Reflection Questions
    • Which storm in my body or mind have I been treating as my own self, when the verse says I am only its background?
    • If misidentification is the only real wound, what specific identification am I most unwilling to release today?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • When a grade, a rejection, or a social-media slight hits hard, pause and label it: this is a cloud crossing the sky — my worth as a soul is untouched.
    • Before scrolling, name one guṇa-driven craving the feed is pulling on (envy, lust, restlessness) and refuse to confuse that pull with who you actually are.
    • Pick one friendship strained by peer pressure and speak to that friend today as a soul, not as a status — let your steadiness, not your performance, do the talking.
    householder
    • In the next family argument, catch the moment your body tenses and your voice rises, and silently re-anchor: I am the sky, this reaction is the wind — then respond, don't react.
    • When a financial or career setback lands, refuse to let the household's mood collapse into it; serve dinner, do sādhana, and treat the setback as weather, not identity.
    • Speak to your children about a difficulty you faced this week as something that passed across you, not something that defined you — model the dhīra-bhāva of this verse.
    senior
    • As the body declines, practice naming each new limitation aloud as belonging to earth, water, and fire — and use that clarity to deepen, not diminish, your daily sādhana.
    • When old regrets or resentments rise like sudden storms, treat them as kāla-sṛṣṭa guṇas passing through, and offer each one to Kṛṣṇa rather than rehearsing them.
    • Mentor a younger seeker this week by showing — not just telling — how a life of struggle can leave the soul's divine qualities being steadily revived, exactly as Madhvācārya describes.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Using sky-like detachment as an excuse for emotional numbness or neglect of duty, instead of clear-eyed engagement from the spiritual platform.
    • Drifting into impersonalist language — 'I am pure awareness' — and forgetting that the soul is Kṛṣṇa's eternal part-and-parcel, not a featureless void.
    • Assuming that because the soul is untouched, the struggle to revive divine qualities can be skipped — Madhvācārya stresses the conditioned soul must still strive.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Share a recent moment when you felt utterly identified with a bodily or mental state — what would it have looked like to stand as the sky in that moment?
    • If the soul is never truly affected, why does Madhvācārya say we must struggle to revive divine qualities? Where might group members honestly disagree on this tension?
    • How is the sky-and-cloud analogy different from the modern 'observe your thoughts' mindfulness teaching, and where could the two be confused?
    Role Play

    One student plays a family member in acute distress over a medical diagnosis, insisting 'this is happening to me.' The other plays a Gauḍīya friend who must respond from this verse — neither denying the body's suffering nor collapsing into it — guiding them to see the soul as the unaffected background while still serving the body compassionately.

    Objections & Responses
    • If the soul is never really affected, then suffering is an illusion and compassion for others' pain is pointless — this teaching sounds cold.
      The verse says the soul is untouched, not that the conditioned experience is unreal. Real compassion serves the soul precisely because we know the body's distress, though superficial, traps the living entity through misidentification — so we act all the more urgently, not less.
    • This sounds like generic non-dualism — the soul as sky, witness behind everything. Why bring Kṛṣṇa into it at all?
      The sky in the analogy is still a created element, and the soul here is explicitly part-and-parcel of Kṛṣṇa, a reservoir of His godly qualities that must be revived. Without Him, 'witnessing' becomes another subtle identification; with Him, it becomes surrender and service.

    • Pick one friendship strained by peer pressure and speak to that friend today as a soul, not as a status — let your steadiness, not your performance, do the talking.
    householder
    • In the next family argument, catch the moment your body tenses and your voice rises, and silently re-anchor: I am the sky, this reaction is the wind — then respond, don't react.
    • When a financial or career setback lands, refuse to let the household's mood collapse into it; serve dinner, do sādhana, and treat the setback as weather, not identity.
    • Speak to your children about a difficulty you faced this week as something that passed across you, not something that defined you — model the dhīra-bhāva of this verse.
    senior
    • As the body declines, practice naming each new limitation aloud as belonging to earth, water, and fire — and use that clarity to deepen, not diminish, your daily sādhana.
    • When old regrets or resentments rise like sudden storms, treat them as kāla-sṛṣṭa guṇas passing through, and offer each one to Kṛṣṇa rather than rehearsing them.
    • Mentor a younger seeker this week by showing — not just telling — how a life of struggle can leave the soul's divine qualities being steadily revived, exactly as Madhvācārya describes.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Using sky-like detachment as an excuse for emotional numbness or neglect of duty, instead of clear-eyed engagement from the spiritual platform.
    • Drifting into impersonalist language — 'I am pure awareness' — and forgetting that the soul is Kṛṣṇa's eternal part-and-parcel, not a featureless void.
    • Assuming that because the soul is untouched, the struggle to revive divine qualities can be skipped — Madhvācārya stresses the conditioned soul must still strive.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Share a recent moment when you felt utterly identified with a bodily or mental state — what would it have looked like to stand as the sky in that moment?
    • If the soul is never truly affected, why does Madhvācārya say we must struggle to revive divine qualities? Where might group members honestly disagree on this tension?
    • How is the sky-and-cloud analogy different from the modern 'observe your thoughts' mindfulness teaching, and where could the two be confused?
    Role Play

    One student plays a family member in acute distress over a medical diagnosis, insisting 'this is happening to me.' The other plays a Gauḍīya friend who must respond from this verse — neither denying the body's suffering nor collapsing into it — guiding them to see the soul as the unaffected background while still serving the body compassionately.

    Objections & Responses
    • If the soul is never really affected, then suffering is an illusion and compassion for others' pain is pointless — this teaching sounds cold.
      The verse says the soul is untouched, not that the conditioned experience is unreal. Real compassion serves the soul precisely because we know the body's distress, though superficial, traps the living entity through misidentification — so we act all the more urgently, not less.
    • This sounds like generic non-dualism — the soul as sky, witness behind everything. Why bring Kṛṣṇa into it at all?
      The sky in the analogy is still a created element, and the soul here is explicitly part-and-parcel of Kṛṣṇa, a reservoir of His godly qualities that must be revived. Without Him, 'witnessing' becomes another subtle identification; with Him, it becomes surrender and service.

    O King, a saintly person is just like water because he is free from all contamination, gentle by nature, and by speaking creates a beautiful vibration like that of flowing water. Just by seeing, touching or hearing such a saintly person, the living entity is purified, just as one is cleansed by contact with pure water. Thus a saintly person, just like a holy place, purifies all those who contact him because he always chants the glories of the Lord.
    Purport

    The words apāṁ mitram, “just like water,” can also be read as aghān mitram, which means that a saintly person purifies all living entities by accepting them as mitram, or his personal friends, and saves them from their sinful reactions ( aghāt ). The conditioned living entity falsely identifies with his gross material body and subtle mind and thus falls from the platform of spiritual knowledge. A conditioned living being is always lusty for material sense gratification, and if he does not acquire it, he becomes angry. Sometimes he is so obsessed with fear of losing his material gratification that he enters a stage approaching madness.

    A saintly person, however, is like pure water, free from all contamination and capable of purifying all things. Just as pure water is transparent, a saintly person transparently manifests the Personality of Godhead within his heart. Such love of Godhead is the reservoir of all happiness. Water makes a most pleasing vibration as it flows and cascades, and similarly the sound vibration of the Lord’s pure devotee, who is saturated with the glories of the Lord, is most charming and beautiful. Thus, by studying the nature of water one can understand the symptoms of a pure devotee of the Lord.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Like water, the devotee is pure by nature, affectionate to people, sweet in speech, and purifying to all people by being seen, touched or glorified. He learns from water. Similar to water (apām mitram), the devotee is pure, by nature friendly to people, speaks sweetly, and purifies people by giving instructions on bhakti. Instead of apām, the word aghād is also found. The sentence then means “He purifies a friend of sin.” He is similar to water which has qualities of purity, friendliness, and purity.

    • Tamohara Pr SB 11-07-44 - 2017-04-14 ISKCON Alachua
      His Grace Tamohara Prabhu· 2017-04-14· English
    • MG SB 11-07-44-45 - Krishna inst Uddhava - 2007-01-07 Rajkot
      His Holiness Mahavishnu Goswami· 2007-01-07· English
    • RGS SB 11-07-44-49 Hindi - Twenty-Four Guru-14
      His Holiness Radha Govinda Swami· English
    Personal Guidance
    A sādhu is like pure water — transparent, gentle, melodious — and purifies whoever sees, touches, or hears him because he constantly chants Kṛṣṇa's glories.
    Practical Applications
    • Seek out one devotee today whose darśana, touch, or speech you can receive, and treat the contact as a real bath for the heart.
    • Audit your own speech this evening: does it flow with Kṛṣṇa's glories like clear water, or does it carry the silt of complaint, gossip, and self-promotion?
    • Refuse to let cynicism dismiss the sādhu as ordinary — approach him as mitram, a friend who actively dissolves your aghān, not as a social acquaintance.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where in my life do I keep choosing muddied association over the transparent water of devotee saṅga, and what am I afraid the clear water will reveal?
    • If a saintly person's purifying power flows specifically through chanting Kṛṣṇa's names and pastimes, what does my own daily speech reveal about whose servant I actually am?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • Pick one feed, group chat, or friend circle this week whose 'water' is muddy with envy and irony, and trade an hour of it for an hour with someone who actually speaks of Kṛṣṇa.
    • When the next exam result, crush, or follower count threatens to tip you into anger or near-madness, name the cascade Prabhupāda describes — lust unmet becomes anger becomes fear — and call or message a devotee before reacting.
    • Stop curating a 'gentle, deep' online persona; instead, in one real conversation today, let your speech carry Kṛṣṇa's name plainly, and see who is drawn closer and who pulls away.
    householder
    • Choose your family's associations the way you choose your drinking water: this month, deliberately bring one sādhu's class, kīrtana, or recorded lecture into the home where your children can see, hear, and touch that current.
    • In the next domestic conflict over money, schooling, or in-laws, refuse the role of the angry, fearful conditioned soul Prabhupāda describes; speak slowly, transparently, and bring Kṛṣṇa's perspective into the room before any decision.
    • Audit your professional speech this week — meetings, emails, negotiations — and replace one habitual stream of self-promotion or complaint with mādhurya: gentle, clear, and, where appropriate, glorifying of the Lord.
    senior
    • Make yourself approachable as water: set a fixed hour each week when children, grandchildren, or younger devotees can simply sit, hear you chant, and ask anything — let darśana, sparśa, and kīrtana do the teaching.
    • Loosen one remaining grip — a property, a grudge, a role you cling to — and notice how quickly transparency returns to your speech once that silt is gone.
    • Use the time aging gives you to become saturated in Kṛṣṇa's glories through daily japa and reading, so that whoever encounters you in your final years contacts not your personality but the Lord seated in your purified heart.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Reducing the verse to 'be a nice, calm person' — missing that the purifying potency comes from saturation in Kṛṣṇa-kīrtana, not from a gentle personality.
    • Treating sādhu-saṅga as aesthetic or social — collecting darśanas like experiences while never letting the sādhu's words actually rearrange your life.
    • Imagining you can purify others by your own goodness before you have become transparent yourself — playing teacher while still carrying lust, anger, and fear of losing enjoyment.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Share one person whose mere presence, touch, or voice has actually purified something in you — and test together whether that effect tracks with this verse's criteria or with something else.
    • Prabhupāda links the conditioned soul's lust, anger, and near-madness to false bodily identification; where do each of you see that progression running in your own week, and would more sādhu-saṅga genuinely interrupt it?
    • Debate honestly: is it possible to be 'svacchaḥ and snigdhaḥ' — transparent and gentle — without chanting Kṛṣṇa's names, or does the verse insist the two cannot be separated?
    Role Play

    One student plays a stressed coworker venting bitterly about a missed promotion; the other must respond as someone trying to embody this verse — svacchaḥ, snigdhaḥ, and weaving in Kṛṣṇa's glories — without moralizing, faking calm, or abandoning real friendship. Afterward, the group examines where the 'water' became muddy and where it actually flowed.

    Objections & Responses
    • This sounds like spiritual bypassing — telling people that just seeing or touching a holy man fixes them, while ignoring therapy, justice, and real psychological work.
      The verse is not promising bodily or emotional repair; it is naming a specific potency — purification of the conditioned identity that drives lust, anger, and fear in the first place. Prabhupāda's purport actually diagnoses the psychological cascade clearly. Therapy and justice address symptoms at the level of mind and society; the sādhu addresses the root misidentification with body and mind. They are not rivals, but the verse refuses to let us pretend the root can be skipped.
    • Calling someone a 'saintly person' who purifies by sight is a recipe for guru-cults and abuse — history is full of such 'holy men' who turned out to be predators.
      Precisely why the verse gives diagnostic symptoms, not a title to grant: svacchaḥ (transparent, hiding nothing), snigdhaḥ (genuinely gentle, not performatively soft), mādhuryaḥ in speech, and constant kīrtana of Kṛṣṇa — not of himself, his lineage's prestige, or his own attainments. A man who fails these tests is, by this very verse, not the sādhu being described. The śāstra is protecting you from cults, not building one.

    Saintly persons become powerful by execution of austerities. Their consciousness is unshakable because they do not try to enjoy anything within the material world. Such naturally liberated sages accept foodstuffs that are offered to them by destiny, and if by chance they happen to eat contaminated food, they are not affected, just like fire, which burns up contaminated substances that are offered to it.
    Purport

    The word udara-bhājana indicates that a saintly person eats only to keep body and soul together and not for sense gratification. One should eat palatable foodstuffs to maintain one’s mind in a cheerful mood; however, one should not eat luxuriously, because this will cause sex desire and laziness. A saintly person is always a perfect gentleman and is never greedy or lusty. Although māyā tries to defeat him by offering different material allurements, ultimately these attractive material features are themselves defeated by the spiritual power of a saintly person. Thus, one should never disrespect a spiritually advanced personality but should worship him reverentially. To carelessly approach a Kṛṣṇa conscious personality is just like carelessly approaching fire, which immediately burns if not handled properly. The Lord does not excuse mistreatment of a pure devotee.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    He who is like fire, who glows with austerity, who cannot be agitated, who eats only enough to fill his stomach, and who is not contaminated though he eats everything, becomes a true yogī. Three verses describe what he learned from fire. He cannot be agitated (durdharṣaḥ) and eats to fill his stomach. He becomes a yogi (yuktātmā).
    Related lectures
    • NRM SB 11-07-45-74
      Her Grace Narayani Mataji· English
    • Balaram Shakti Pr SB 11-07-45-51 - GEV
      His Grace Balaram Shakti Prabhu· English
    Personal Guidance
    Like fire that consumes impurity untouched, a sage tempered by tapasya takes only what destiny sends and is not contaminated by what passes through him.
    Practical Applications
    • Eat today only what is needed to keep body and soul fit for service — refuse the second helping that feeds laziness or lust.
    • Accept whatever simple food, work, or circumstance comes to you today as sent by Kṛṣṇa, without scheming for something tastier or grander.
    • Approach any advanced devotee in your life with reverence today — speak less, listen more, and never address them casually as a peer.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where am I using 'I am detached like fire' as a private license to consume things I have no business consuming?
    • What austerity have I been quietly avoiding because I prefer the warmth of comfort to the heat of real tapasya?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • At the next hostel mess or hangout, eat a normal portion of what is served and stop — do not scroll the delivery app afterward looking for something more exciting.
    • Notice the urge to argue back or crack a joke when a senior devotee or teacher corrects you, and instead say 'thank you' and sit with it for a day before responding.
    • Refuse the social-media game of curating an 'authentic detached' image — post less, perform purity less, and quietly do one austerity no one sees.
    householder
    • Plan the family meals this week around what is simple, offerable, and nourishing — not around what impresses guests or soothes your own restlessness after work.
    • When a financial or career opportunity arrives that you did not chase, weigh it as something destiny has offered, and accept or decline based on dharma rather than appetite.
    • Bring your children into the presence of a genuine devotee this month, and model for them what reverential approach — not casual familiarity — looks like.
    senior
    • Simplify your diet now in a way you have been postponing — fewer luxuries, smaller portions — so the body remains a fit udara-bhājana for chanting and study.
    • Stop arranging your circumstances so carefully; accept the room, the food, and the help your family or āśrama provides as Kṛṣṇa's arrangement, and let go of the editor's pen.
    • Mentor a younger devotee specifically in how to approach advanced Vaiṣṇavas — not as peers, not as service-providers, but as fire that must be honored from the proper distance.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Imagining oneself already fire-like and therefore immune, while still being a piece of damp wood that contamination genuinely soaks into.
    • Reading udara-bhājana as permission for monkish self-neglect, starving the body until the mind becomes morose instead of cheerful in service.
    • Treating a Kṛṣṇa conscious personality casually — joking, arguing, or testing them — under the modern notion that all relationships should be flat and informal.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Share one specific food, comfort, or indulgence you tell yourself is 'fine because you are detached' — and let the group press on whether that is actually true.
    • Where in your life are you closer to a saint who accepts what comes, and where are you closer to someone who quietly arranges his own menu while claiming surrender?
    • Tell the group about a senior devotee you have approached carelessly — what happened, and what would reverential approach have looked like instead?
    Role Play

    A friend invites you to a dinner where the food's origin is unclear and possibly not offered to Kṛṣṇa. One student plays a young devotee who quotes this verse to justify eating freely 'like fire'; another plays a thoughtful older devotee who must respond — neither rigidly refusing nor naively agreeing — drawing out what udara-bhājana and yuktātmā actually require here.

    Objections & Responses
    • This verse just sounds like spiritual bypassing — 'sages can do anything and stay pure.' Isn't it dangerous to teach this?
      The verse describes the yuktātmā, one whose consciousness is already unshakable because he is not trying to enjoy. It is a description of an attained state, not a permission slip for beginners. For us, the practical instruction is the opposite — eat simply, accept what comes, and revere those who have actually become fire-like. Mistaking ourselves for the fire is precisely how we get burned.
    • Modern nutrition science says we should carefully curate what we eat. Isn't 'accept whatever destiny brings' irresponsible?
      Prabhupāda is clear that one should eat palatable, wholesome food to keep the mind cheerful — not anything at all. The point is not indifference to the body but freedom from greed and luxury. A devotee plans sensibly, offers his food to Kṛṣṇa, and then receives the result as prasāda — that is yukta-āhāra, neither careless nor neurotic.

    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • At the next hostel mess or hangout, eat a normal portion of what is served and stop — do not scroll the delivery app afterward looking for something more exciting.
    • Notice the urge to argue back or crack a joke when a senior devotee or teacher corrects you, and instead say 'thank you' and sit with it for a day before responding.
    • Refuse the social-media game of curating an 'authentic detached' image — post less, perform purity less, and quietly do one austerity no one sees.
    householder
    • Plan the family meals this week around what is simple, offerable, and nourishing — not around what impresses guests or soothes your own restlessness after work.
    • When a financial or career opportunity arrives that you did not chase, weigh it as something destiny has offered, and accept or decline based on dharma rather than appetite.
    • Bring your children into the presence of a genuine devotee this month, and model for them what reverential approach — not casual familiarity — looks like.
    senior
    • Simplify your diet now in a way you have been postponing — fewer luxuries, smaller portions — so the body remains a fit udara-bhājana for chanting and study.
    • Stop arranging your circumstances so carefully; accept the room, the food, and the help your family or āśrama provides as Kṛṣṇa's arrangement, and let go of the editor's pen.
    • Mentor a younger devotee specifically in how to approach advanced Vaiṣṇavas — not as peers, not as service-providers, but as fire that must be honored from the proper distance.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Imagining oneself already fire-like and therefore immune, while still being a piece of damp wood that contamination genuinely soaks into.
    • Reading udara-bhājana as permission for monkish self-neglect, starving the body until the mind becomes morose instead of cheerful in service.
    • Treating a Kṛṣṇa conscious personality casually — joking, arguing, or testing them — under the modern notion that all relationships should be flat and informal.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Share one specific food, comfort, or indulgence you tell yourself is 'fine because you are detached' — and let the group press on whether that is actually true.
    • Where in your life are you closer to a saint who accepts what comes, and where are you closer to someone who quietly arranges his own menu while claiming surrender?
    • Tell the group about a senior devotee you have approached carelessly — what happened, and what would reverential approach have looked like instead?
    Role Play

    A friend invites you to a dinner where the food's origin is unclear and possibly not offered to Kṛṣṇa. One student plays a young devotee who quotes this verse to justify eating freely 'like fire'; another plays a thoughtful older devotee who must respond — neither rigidly refusing nor naively agreeing — drawing out what udara-bhājana and yuktātmā actually require here.

    Objections & Responses
    • This verse just sounds like spiritual bypassing — 'sages can do anything and stay pure.' Isn't it dangerous to teach this?
      The verse describes the yuktātmā, one whose consciousness is already unshakable because he is not trying to enjoy. It is a description of an attained state, not a permission slip for beginners. For us, the practical instruction is the opposite — eat simply, accept what comes, and revere those who have actually become fire-like. Mistaking ourselves for the fire is precisely how we get burned.
    • Modern nutrition science says we should carefully curate what we eat. Isn't 'accept whatever destiny brings' irresponsible?
      Prabhupāda is clear that one should eat palatable, wholesome food to keep the mind cheerful — not anything at all. The point is not indifference to the body but freedom from greed and luxury. A devotee plans sensibly, offers his food to Kṛṣṇa, and then receives the result as prasāda — that is yukta-āhāra, neither careless nor neurotic.
